title: The best La Growth Machine alternatives in 2026
summary: La Growth Machine alternatives for 2026, ranked. Artisan writes, sends, and answers outreach for you, plus Lemlist, Reply, Smartlead and more.
body_text: The best La Growth Machine alternative for most teams is Artisan, because it does the part La Growth Machine leaves to you: Ava, its AI business development representative (BDR), writes the multichannel outreach, sends it with managed deliverability, and answers the replies autonomously. La Growth Machine builds elegant sequences. You still run them. La Growth Machine earned its following on social-first multichannel outreach: one sequence spanning email, LinkedIn, and calls, orchestrated per sending identity. This model is smart, and for a small team that likes steering its own campaigns it holds up well. But its per-identity pricing scales with the number of personas you send from, and the writing, targeting, and reply-handling stay your job. Teams shopping for an alternative usually want less of that manual load, not a prettier way to carry it. La Growth Machine alternatives compared Rank Tool Best for Standout capability Public pricing 1 Artisan Teams that want multichannel outreach written, sent, and answered for them Ava, an autonomous AI BDR with managed deliverability Usage-based credits, no platform fee, free trial 2 Lemlist Personalization-first multichannel sequences Custom images and variables across channels $69-109/user/month 3 Reply Teams that want an AI agent on top of sequencing Jason AI agent plus multichannel cadences Sequences from $59/mo; AI agent tier about $500-800/mo 4 Smartlead Agencies that run many client inboxes Unlimited mailbox rotation, deep API $39-379/mo (placement testing extra) 5 Woodpecker Small teams that want usage-based sending Pay-per-prospect pricing, unlimited inboxes About $7 per 100 prospects contacted 6 Saleshandy Teams starting outbound on a tight budget Lead finder bundled with sending Published per-tier pricing How we chose Four criteria, weighted for a buyer who is tired of running multichannel campaigns by hand: 1. How much of the job the tool does. Sequencing across channels is table stakes now. The real question is whether the tool writes and replies, or just schedules the words you supply. 2. Deliverability at scale. Mailbox provisioning and management, inbox placement testing, sender reputation monitoring, and automatic pausing of unhealthy mailboxes. 3. Pricing transparency and shape. Published tiers beat quote-on-request, and we flag per-identity or per-seat models that tax growth. 4. Deployment fit. Whether one operator can run it, or whether it needs a dedicated specialist steering every persona. Why do teams look for a La Growth Machine alternative? Most switch because La Growth Machine's model is orchestration-first, and orchestration is only half the job. It gives you a clean canvas for multichannel sequences and lets you assign each one to a sending identity. What it does not do is invent the messaging, choose the accounts, or work the inbox once replies land. This is a fair trade if you have people who enjoy that work. It is a poor one if the reason you bought software was to stop doing it. The triggers we hear most: The manual load doesn't shrink. You still write each variant, build the branching logic, and answer every reply by hand. More channels can mean more places to keep up with, not fewer. Per-identity pricing taxes scale. Because the model bills per sending persona, cost rises every time you add a rep or a mailbox, which pinches teams trying to widen their footprint. Social-first is a strength and a ceiling. The multichannel design shines for high-touch, low-volume motions. Teams that need real email volume alongside it often bolt on a second tool. Our guide to cold emailing covers that email side. None of this makes La Growth Machine a weak product. It makes it the wrong product for a team that wants outbound to run without a person steering every persona. The best La Growth Machine alternatives in 2026 1. Artisan: The AI BDR that writes, sends, and replies Artisan is the alternative for teams that want the outbound job owned rather than orchestrated. Instead of a sequence canvas you fill in, Artisan gives you Ava, an autonomous AI BDR. Ava finds best-fit leads from a database of over 250 million B2B professionals across over 200 countries, plus Artisan Local Data with over 250 million local businesses, then writes personalized multichannel outreach across email, social media, and dialer call steps, sends it with managed deliverability, and handles the replies: qualifying, answering objections from your knowledge base, chasing follow-ups, and booking meetings on your reps' calendars. Two people in the same campaign receive two different messages, not a swapped first name. Calls are a genuine step rather than a bolt-on. Ava dials for your reps with power and parallel dialing across up to three lines, AI answer detection, live transcription, and native CRM logging, and a rep takes the live conversation from there. The deliverability layer is where the La Growth Machine comparison sharpens. Artisan provisions and manages mailboxes, tests inbox placement, checks SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records, watches mailbox health, applies dynamic send limits, rotates inboxes, and auto-pauses senders that start bouncing. You tune none of it by hand. Autonomy is adjustable rather than binary: review and approve every message, restrict Ava to objection-handling, or let her run fully autonomous with plain-language escalation rules and a full audit trail. Artisan reports over 90% of customers run Ava autonomously. For larger teams, the deployment pattern matters as much as the features. Sales ops can run Ava centrally for an account executive (AE) team whose reps never log in, with cross-channel do-not-contact enforcement and CRM owner routing so outreach comes from the right rep's mailbox. Artisan is SOC 2 Type II compliant, GDPR and CCPA compliant, with single sign-on (SSO) and role-based access on Enterprise plans. Pricing is usage-based rather than per identity, so widening your footprint does not multiply a subscription. "At SumUp, we prioritize efficient and scalable growth. Artisan's platform streamlines our outreach and gives us the insights we need to reach the right businesses in meaningful ways," said Karlo Biuk, Growth Lead at SumUp, whose team ran Ava at a $52 cost per lead and 8 to 15 positive replies a week from local businesses. See Artisan pricing for the current model. Best for: startups through enterprise that want multichannel outreach written, sent, and answered autonomously, with deliverability managed for them. Who should pick something else: small teams that specifically enjoy hand-building tight multichannel sequences and want to steer each persona themselves. Pricing: usage-based credits, no platform fee, free trial. See artisan.co/pricing . 2. Lemlist: Personalization-first multichannel Lemlist is the closest like-for-like alternative for a team that loves La Growth Machine's multichannel design but wants stronger personalization craft. It pioneered custom images and dynamic variables inside outreach and runs sequences that combine email with LinkedIn steps. Bootstrapped to roughly $40M in revenue and having acquired the video tool Claap in October 2025, it is a serious independent company with real personalization pedigree. The trade is that Lemlist's personalization is powerful but manual: you build the tokens, images, and logic yourself. It scales your creativity, not your headcount. Pricing runs $69 to $109/user/month, per its pricing page. For head-to-head breakdowns, see Artisan vs. Lemlist and Apollo vs. Lemlist . Best for: teams that want visually crafted multichannel sequences and will invest the time to build them. Who should pick something else: teams that want the personalization generated for them at scale. See our roundup of the best cold email tools . Pricing: $69-109/user/month, per Lemlist's pricing page. 3. Reply: An AI agent on a sequencer Reply is the pick for a team that wants an AI agent layered onto multichannel cadences without leaving the sequencer world. Its Jason AI agent drafts messages and handles some reply logic on top of Reply's email and multichannel sequences. For teams moving cautiously from manual sequencing toward agent-run email, it is an accessible on-ramp. The limit is that Jason is an email-centric agent sitting on a classic sequencer, so a human still owns much of the motion. Reply's platform sequences start around $59 per month, with its AI agent tier at roughly $500 to $800 per month, per Reply's pricing pages. Best for: teams that want a light AI agent bolted onto familiar multichannel sequencing. Who should pick something else: teams that want the sourcing, writing, and replying owned end to end rather than assisted. Pricing: sequences from about $59/mo; AI agent tier about $500-800/mo, per Reply's pricing pages. 4. Smartlead: The agency and API workhorse Smartlead is the alternative for volume email operators and agencies, especially those that run many client inboxes. Unlimited mailbox rotation, a deep API, and a master inbox for many accounts make it strong where La Growth Machine's per-identity social focus is not. If your business sends on behalf of other businesses, Smartlead's architecture fits. The cost math needs a note: core tiers run $39 to $379 per month, but placement testing is billed separately at $49 to $599, so the effective price climbs once you turn on serious-sender features. And like La Growth Machine, Smartlead is infrastructure. You still write and reply. For a broader comparison, see our roundup of outbound sales tools . Best for: agencies and API-first teams that run many inboxes at email volume. Who should pick something else: teams that want multichannel depth or the copy and replies handled. Pricing: $39-379/mo core; placement testing $49-599 extra, per Smartlead's pricing page. 5. Woodpecker: Simple usage-based sending Woodpecker is the pick for small teams that want predictable pricing and unlimited inboxes without a per-seat or per-identity model. It charges about $7 per 100 prospects contacted, which suits spiky or seasonal volume. Deliverability tooling is solid and the interface stays out of your way. Woodpecker is deliberately narrower than La Growth Machine. It is a focused email sequencer, lighter on multichannel and AI. For a small team that mostly wants reliable, affordable email, this focus is a feature. See our roundup of the best email outbound tools for more. Best for: small teams that want usage pricing and unlimited inboxes. Who should pick something else: teams that need deep multichannel orchestration or the work done for them. Pricing: usage-based, about $7 per 100 prospects contacted, per Woodpecker's pricing page. 6. Saleshandy: The budget entry point Saleshandy is the value pick for teams starting outbound on a tight budget. It bundles a lead finder with sending and sequencing at published, low per-tier prices, so you can prospect and send from one place without stitching in a separate lead source. For a first outbound motion, this is a useful consolidation. The ceiling is the manual model. Saleshandy sends what you write and leaves replies for you to handle, and its multichannel story is thin next to La Growth Machine's. It is a fine starting rung teams tend to outgrow. If email is your focus, compare the best cold email marketing software . Best for: teams launching a first outbound motion on a tight budget. Who should pick something else: teams that want multichannel depth or autonomous writing and replies. Pricing: published per-tier pricing, per Saleshandy's pricing page. Stay with La Growth Machine if... La Growth Machine is the right call for a specific profile. Keep it if: You run high-touch, lower-volume multichannel motions and enjoy hand-crafting each sequence. Your persona count is small, so per-identity pricing stays affordable. Social-first outreach on LinkedIn is central to how you sell, and email volume is secondary. Switching tools to fix a copy-and-reply problem that La Growth Machine was never built to solve is a mistake. If the manual load is the problem, this is the signal to move to an autonomous AI BDR instead. Frequently asked questions What is the best alternative to La Growth Machine? For teams that want multichannel outreach written, sent, and answered for them, Artisan is the strongest alternative, because Ava runs the full job autonomously with managed deliverability. For a like-for-like multichannel sequencer with stronger personalization craft, Lemlist is the closest direct rival. What is the best enterprise alternative to La Growth Machine? Artisan. It adds what larger teams need on top of sequencing: central sales-ops deployment for AE teams who never log in, cross-channel do-not-contact governance, CRM owner routing, an audit trail, and SOC 2 Type II compliance. La Growth Machine's per-identity model is built for hands-on operators rather than governed at-scale deployment. How does La Growth Machine's per-identity pricing work? La Growth Machine bills per sending identity, roughly one persona's email and LinkedIn accounts, so your cost rises with each rep or mailbox you add. Usage-based pricing like Artisan's, where you pay for work performed rather than per persona, keeps costs from multiplying as you widen your footprint. Is Lemlist better than La Growth Machine? For personalization depth, often yes: Lemlist's custom images and variables are stronger. Both are manual multichannel sequencers with the same limit, though. You still write and reply. Lemlist runs $69 to $109/user/month. Can I replace La Growth Machine with an AI SDR? Yes, if you want the job done rather than the sequence enabled. An autonomous AI sales agent like Ava, an AI sales development representative (SDR), sources leads, writes multichannel outreach, manages deliverability, and answers replies, which covers La Growth Machine's function plus the manual work it leaves to you. Which La Growth Machine alternative is cheapest? Woodpecker's usage model (about $7 per 100 prospects contacted) and Saleshandy's low published tiers are the most budget-friendly at small volumes. Cheapest per message is not the same as cheapest per meeting booked, which is where autonomous tools change the math. Does La Growth Machine handle replies for me? No. La Growth Machine sequences outreach across channels, but qualifying and answering replies is your job. This reply-handling gap is the main reason teams evaluating Artisan look past sequencers toward an autonomous BDR. Related reading Apollo vs. Instantly Artisan vs. Instantly

title: How to Learn a Language While Commuting (August 2026)
summary: Get real language practice from your daily commute in August 2026. Find out which audio methods work for walking, driving, and riding transit hands-free.
body_text: Twenty minutes a day of the right kind of practice beats two hours on a Saturday that you forget by Wednesday, and most people already have those 20 minutes baked into their day. The tricky part is that learning a language while commuting means something different depending on whether you're behind the wheel, on foot, or on a train. Each mode has its own constraints, and working with them instead of against them is what makes daily reps stick. TLDR: Your average round-trip commute adds up to roughly 45 hours of monthly practice time you're currently not using for language learning. Twenty minutes daily beats two hours on Saturday because a meta-analysis of 48 spacing experiments found spaced practice produces measurably better delayed retention than massed study sessions. Walking gives you the most productive reps since your hands and eyes are free; a 2014 Goethe University Frankfurt study found vocabulary encoded during light walking outperformed seated study. Most apps marketed as commute-friendly fail the two real tests: lock-screen playback and advancing without a tap. Most apps in the comparison table below fail one or both. ISSEN's AI voice tutor runs in background mode with smart turn detection across 60+ languages, making it one of the few options that works while your phone stays in your pocket. Your commute is already a language classroom The average one-way commute in the United States runs 27.2 minutes , which adds up to roughly 45 hours a month for a round-trip five-day week. Most of that time gets spent half-listening to a podcast or watching brake lights. Speaking and listening are ears-and-mouth skills. They do not need a screen or a desk. That makes commutes well-suited for the part of language learning traditional study leaves underdeveloped, which is why AI language apps for busy adults have focused on audio-first formats.: producing sound out loud and processing it in real time. Walking, driving, and transit each carry different constraints, and the rest of this piece works through them one by one. Can you learn a language while driving? Yes, driving is one of the oldest ways adults have picked up languages outside a classroom. The catch is that only listening-based methods work safely behind the wheel: audio lessons, native dialogue tracks, and spoken repetition drills that ask nothing of your eyes or hands. This lines up with Krashen's input hypothesis, which holds that acquisition happens when you take in language slightly above your current level in meaningful context. A dialogue between two native speakers about renting an apartment counts. A grammar exercise on your phone does not. What actually works in the car: Graded audio lessons where a host prompts you to repeat phrases aloud Native-speaker podcasts pitched at your level or one notch above Audiobooks you have already read in translation, so the plot carries you through unfamiliar words Shadowing short lines from a track you have heard before What does not work: tapping through flashcards, reading subtitles, and any grammar drill that assumes you can look at a screen. How many minutes of commuting per day is enough? Twenty minutes a day, five days a week, is enough to make measurable progress. That gives you about 100 minutes of weekly exposure, and a 30-minute one-way ride puts you in the 150 to 250 minute range most self-taught learners maintain long term. Daily beats weekly because of spacing. A meta-analysis of 48 spacing experiments found medium-to-large benefits for spaced review over massed practice, especially for delayed retention. Two hours on Saturday feels productive and evaporates by Wednesday. Twenty minutes Monday through Friday builds the retrieval loops that stick. Start with the commute you already have. You do not need to add time to your day. Is it safe to practice speaking while driving? Speaking out loud while driving is a gray zone worth taking seriously. The CDC groups distracted driving into three types : visual, manual, and cognitive. Cognitive load still pulls attention off the road even when your hands are free. The practical rule: Passive listening to audio courses, podcasts, or dialogue tracks is fine while driving. Repeating a short phrase after a prompt works on an empty highway, not in city traffic. Full conversation practice or sentence construction belongs on walks, transit rides, or a parked car before you pull out. Hands-free still carries cognitive load. Save the harder reps for moments your eyes are not doing safety work. What is the best way to practice a language while walking? Walking is the strongest commute mode for active practice because your mouth and ears are free while your hands and eyes stay engaged with the sidewalk. A 2014 study at Goethe University Frankfurt found that adults who encoded vocabulary during light treadmill walking outperformed those who studied seated. That opens room for harder reps a car ride cannot support: Shadowing native audio out loud, matching rhythm and stress as you step Full voice conversations through earbuds with an AI voice tutor Podcast episodes where you pause and repeat lines back Narrating what you see around you in the target language A 25-minute walk handles a full session end to end. How do you learn a language hands-free without looking at your phone? The setup takes about five minutes the first time and zero after that. Do it once at home, and every commute after runs without you touching your phone. Pre-load audio the night before. Download podcast episodes, audiobook chapters, or lesson tracks so nothing buffers on cellular or drops in a tunnel. Pair Bluetooth earbuds you can control by touch. Play, pause, and skip should live on the earbud, not the screen. Turn on lock-screen playback. If a session pauses when your phone locks, it fails the commute test. Pick tools that advance without taps. Audio courses and voice tutors that run in the background belong in the rotation. Flashcard apps that require swiping do not. Seated transit riders get one bonus: a subway ride lets you add a transcript or saved sentence list without any safety tradeoff. Standing on a crowded train, keep your eyes up and treat it like a walking session. What to listen to: audio formats ranked by commute value Match the format to your level and where you are. A quick ranked view: Format Best for Commute mode Structured audio courses (Pimsleur, Language Transfer) A0 to A2 beginners Driving, walking, transit Native dialogue recordings for learners A2 to B1 Driving, walking, transit Learner podcasts with graded input A2 to B1 Driving, walking, transit Native news, interviews, and audiobooks B1 and up Driving, walking, transit Live AI voice conversation Any level with productive intent Walking or parked only The higher the production demand, the more your eyes and hands need to be free. Save live conversation for the sidewalk. How to build a consistent language learning habit long term The commute itself is the trigger. You do not decide to practice, you start the session when you start the walk or the engine. Habit stacking works because it removes the daily choice. A few anchors: Set a minimum viable session of 10 minutes. If that is all you have, it still counts. Track spoken output minutes, not streaks or lessons finished. Streaks reward opening an app; minutes reward using your mouth, which is why speaking practice in your language routine deserves its own dedicated slot. Match the mode to the day, and when you miss one, move on without renegotiating the whole plan. Driving days lean listening, walking days lean speaking, transit days handle either. Hands-free language app comparison 2026 Not every app that markets voice practice actually works when your phone is in your pocket; a broader look at language learning apps with AI voice shows how wide the gap is. The table below measures six apps against four commute-specific criteria. Verify current capabilities on each app's store listing before subscribing. App Runs with screen locked Advances without tapping Passive listening mode Voice-only sessions ISSEN Yes Yes Yes Yes Duolingo No No Limited (Stories audio) Max tier only Speak No No Yes (lessons) Push-to-talk Pingo Partial No Limited Push-to-talk Memrise No No Yes (Immerse videos) No Babbel No No Yes (Babbel Live audio) No The two questions that matter most for a real commute are lock-screen playback and whether the app moves forward without a tap. Most best language learning apps for speaking still fail one or both. ISSEN: AI voice tutoring built for the commute The commute is where a voice tutor earns its keep, and that gap is exactly what ISSEN was built to fill. The app runs with your screen locked in background mode, so a walking session continues while your phone stays in your pocket. Smart turn detection removes the push-to-talk button: you speak, the tutor waits, then responds. That is a core feature of how AI speaking practice works at its best.A few specifics that matter on a sidewalk or a train: The tutor drives the conversation from the start, so you never have to invent a prompt at a crosswalk. Difficulty adjusts in real time, holding vocabulary and pace at your level within a single turn. Memory carries across sessions. Tuesday's walk picks up from Monday's bus ride without rebuilding context. 60+ languages supported, with flat pricing of $20 to $29 USD per month and unlimited daily practice. If daily reps are the missing layer in a stack that already includes reading, flashcards, or a weekly human tutor, this is where a commute converts into spoken output. Try ISSEN free for 10 minutes. Final thoughts on using your commute to learn a language The 27-minute average commute is not a constraint on language learning. For most self-taught learners, it covers the daily minimum. Driving gets you the input, walking gets you the output, and transit handles whichever one you skipped. Build the habit around the commute you already have, not the study schedule you keep meaning to start. Try ISSEN free for 10 minutes on your next walk. FAQs Can you really learn a language while commuting, or does it only work for passive listening? You can build real productive skills during a commute, but the method has to match the mode. Driving limits you to listening-based practice: audio courses, native dialogue tracks, shadowing short phrases. Walking frees your mouth for full voice conversations, including live back-and-forth with an AI tutor like ISSEN. How much commute time per week do you actually need to make progress in a language? Twenty minutes a day, five days a week, is enough to see measurable gains. A meta-analysis of 48 spacing experiments found medium-to-large retention benefits for distributed practice over massed sessions, which means five short commutes beat one long Saturday study block for building the retrieval loops that stick. Is it safe to practice speaking out loud while driving? Passive listening is fine behind the wheel, but full conversation practice carries real cognitive load. The CDC categorizes cognitive distraction as one of three types of distracted driving, and that load does not disappear when your hands are free. Save sentence construction and live AI conversations for your walk, transit ride, or a parked car before you pull out. Pimsleur vs ISSEN for commute-based language learning? Pimsleur is purpose-built for audio repetition and works well on drives at A0 to B1, but the format is fixed and cannot respond to you. ISSEN runs in background mode with smart turn detection, so a walking commute becomes a live two-way conversation instead of a prompted drill. That is the difference between rehearsing lines and actually speaking under pressure. How do I set up a language learning app to run hands-free during my commute? Do the setup once at home the night before: download audio or lesson content offline, pair Bluetooth earbuds with touch controls, and confirm the app continues from the lock screen. Most speaking apps fail that last test. They pause when your screen locks, which breaks a walking or transit session the moment your phone goes to sleep.

title: Scrap Happens: Turning Industrial Metal Waste Into Recovered Value
summary: Prepare for back-to-school season by reducing waste through system-wide strategies, optimizing efficiency, sustainability, and cost savings.
body_text: Home » Blog » Scrap Happens: Turning Industrial Metal Waste Into Recovered Value Scrap Happens: Turning Industrial Metal Waste Into Recovered Value August 13, 2026 Most industrial operations with real scrap volume already have a vendor, a container and a pickup schedule. But having a program is not the same as maximizing what that program returns. The metals your purchasing team once bought as a capital investment—raw material, tooling, equipment—eventually exit through the back door as scrap. When that happens, responsibility often shifts from procurement to EHS, Facilities Management or Operations. And in that handoff, the focus on recovering full value can quietly disappear. That approach costs you twice. You pay to manage a material that holds genuine market value, and you miss the revenue that same material could return. Here’s how to recognize the problem and turn it into an advantage. Where Investment Recovery Begins Every metal that leaves your facility as scrap once entered it as an asset—purchased by your procurement team, assigned a value and put to work. Copper, aluminum, steel, brass and stainless don’t lose that worth when they reach end of life. They simply change form. Treating them through an asset recovery or investment recovery lens means recognizing that value and building a program designed to capture it. Without that discipline, recoverable worth slips away through a few common gaps: Inadequate segregation. Mixing high-value metals with low-grade scrap collapses your return to the lowest common denominator. Proper sorting by metal type at the source is the single fastest way to increase what your program pays back. Missing or unverified documentation. Every load should come with a state-certified scale ticket showing gross, tare and net weights. Without it, you have no way to verify what left your facility, no paper trail for compliance and no defense against potential abuses. Undersized or mismatched equipment. The right baler, chopper, wire-stripper, compactor or drum crusher can dramatically increase the density and purity of your material—and therefore its value. Running the wrong equipment for your volume or material mix quietly costs you on every load. Poor buyer selection. Not all scrap buyers are equal, and not all are the right fit for your specific materials. Some end-users actively seek particular grades or alloys and will pay a premium to secure them. Settling for the nearest or most convenient buyer rarely gets you the best return. Hidden freight economics. In the scrap business, the generator typically bears freight costs—whether those costs are disclosed or buried in a lower net price. Understanding the true logistics picture is essential to evaluating what your program actually returns versus what it appears to return. Individually, these gaps seem minor. Across a full year of operations, they add up to significant lost revenue and unnecessary cost. The Levers That Separate a Good Program From a Great One Segregation, grading, and equipment right-sizing. Sorting materials correctly at the source is the foundation of every strong scrap program. When high-value metals are separated from lower-grade material, you capture the true market rate for each rather than settling for a blended average. Equipment matters just as much: the right baler, chopper, wire-stripper, compactor or drum crusher increases material density and purity, which directly raises your return. Proper buyer selection and marketing. Not all scrap buyers offer the same value, and finding the right end-user for your specific material—one who actively seeks that grade or alloy—can significantly increase what your program returns. Beyond pricing, logistics is often the single biggest factor in net recovery. Generators typically bear freight costs, whether those costs are clearly disclosed or quietly embedded in a lower offered price. Understanding the true logistics picture is essential to evaluating what your program actually earns versus what it appears to earn on paper. Documentation, chain of custody, and certified destruction. Every load that leaves your facility should be accompanied by a state-certified scale ticket showing gross, tare and net weights. But accountability doesn’t stop at the gate. Quest verifies the entire chain of custody and final disposition of your scrap—giving you a complete, auditable record of where your material went and how it was handled. For generators with proprietary scrap they cannot allow back into the market—whether for competitive, regulatory or brand-protection reasons—Quest can also design and implement a certified destruction process, ensuring that sensitive material is permanently and verifiably eliminated rather than resold or reused. How Quest Maximizes What Your Scrap Program Returns Quest manages more than 100 waste streams for industrial operations across the country, and scrap metal asset recovery is a discipline where our expertise delivers measurable results. We work with generators who already have a program in place to sharpen every element of it—tightening segregation, right-sizing equipment, improving buyer selection, bringing full transparency to freight and logistics, and verifying the complete chain of custody from pickup through final disposition. The goal is not simply to move your scrap. It is to make sure your program returns everything that material is worth—and that every step along the way is documented, controlled and accountable. Our approach rests on a few core strengths: Program evaluation and benchmarking. We assess your existing scrap program against what it should be returning—identifying gaps in segregation, documentation, equipment and buyer relationships so you have a clear picture of where value is being lost. Certified documentation and weight accountability. Every load Quest manages is supported by certified scale tickets showing gross, tare and net weights, protecting you from discrepancies and giving you audit-ready records your program demands. Certified destruction for proprietary scrap. When certain materials cannot be allowed back into the market, Quest designs and implements a certified destruction process—with full documentation—so sensitive scrap is eliminated, not resold. Chain of custody verification. We track and verify the complete disposition of your scrap from pickup through final processing, so you always know exactly where your material went and how it was handled. Equipment right-sizing. We evaluate whether your current containers and processing equipment match your actual material mix and volume—and help you implement the right tools where they’ll make a measurable difference. Scrap marketing and buyer selection. We connect your materials to the right buyers and end-users, including those actively seeking specific grades or alloys, to maximize your net return. Logistics and freight optimization. We bring full transparency to the logistics picture, structuring pickups and routing so those costs work in your favor. Dedicated account management. A committed team monitors program performance, tracks recovery data and refines your approach over time. Having a scrap program is a start—but it’s rarely the whole story. Even well-established programs can quietly underperform through weak documentation, mismatched buyers, hidden freight costs or missed processing efficiencies. If any of those gaps exist in yours, value is leaving your facility that you’ll never get back. The good news: closing those gaps doesn’t require starting over. The process is easier than you’d think: share where you are today and what you want to achieve, and we’ll design a program built around your goals. Ready to maximize what your scrap program actually returns? Contact Quest today.

body_text: Record Quarterly Revenues of $1.26 Billion, a 111% Increase from a Year Ago Excluding Bowers Acquisition, Revenues (non-GAAP) Grew by 60% from a Year Ago1 Quarterly Adjusted EBITDA (non-GAAP) Increased 114% from Prior Year2 Record Total Backlog and Awarded Contracts of $5.67 Billion, a 105% Increase from a Year Ago Establish Third Quarter 2026 Guidance for Revenue of $1.225 Billion - $1.275 Billion and Non-GAAP Adjusted EBITDA of $150 Million - $160 Million Raise Full Year 2026 Guidance for Revenue to $4.7 Billion - $4.8 Billion and Non-GAAP Adjusted EBITDA of $565 Million - $585 Million SAN JOSE, Calif., Aug. 13, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Legence Corp. (Nasdaq: LGN) (“Legence” or the “Company”) today reported financial results for the second quarter ended June 30, 2026. “Strong customer demand led to another record quarter for Legence, with new highs in revenue, Adjusted EBITDA and backlog and awarded contracts,” said Jeff Sprau, Chief Executive Officer of Legence. “Total revenue more than doubled year over year, with revenue growth, excluding the impact of The Bowers Group ("Bowers") acquisition, of approximately 60%. While the data centers & technology end market continues to be a significant driver of our performance, we are also benefitting from healthy activity across our other diverse end markets, including life sciences & healthcare, state & local government, and education. Our dedicated craftspeople, technicians, and engineering professionals are executing at the highest standards, and we are leveraging the scalability of our growth platform to drive sequential Adjusted EBITDA Margin expansion. As we enter the second half of 2026, healthy industry conditions, combined with our backlog-supported visibility, gives us confidence to raise our revenue and profit outlook for the year.” Second Quarter 2026 Consolidated Results: Revenues for the second quarter 2026 totaled $1.26 billion, an increase of 110.7% from $598.9 million for the second quarter 2025. Excluding the impact of the Bowers acquisition, non-GAAP revenue growth was 60.0%. Gross profit for the second quarter 2026 was $220.2 million with gross margin of 17.4%, compared to gross profit of $128.7 million and gross margin of 21.5% for the second quarter 2025. Excluding the impact of compensation related to legacy Series A Interests and Restricted Series C Interests paid for by entities outside of Legence, we generated non-GAAP Adjusted Gross Profit of $234.0 million and non-GAAP Adjusted Gross Margin of 18.5% for the second quarter 2026, compared to non-GAAP Adjusted Gross Profit of $130.3 million and non-GAAP Adjusted Gross Margin of 21.8% for the second quarter 2025. The decrease in non-GAAP Adjusted Gross Profit and non-GAAP Adjusted Gross Margin was primarily due to a revenue mix shift towards Installation & Maintenance and a slight decline in Engineering & Consulting Adjusted Gross Margin. Net loss attributable to Legence for the second quarter 2026 was $27.8 million, or $(0.37) per diluted share, compared to a net loss attributable to Legence of $5.3 million for the second quarter 2025. Net loss for the second quarter 2026 was $34.6 million, compared to a net loss of $3.9 million for the second quarter 2025. Non-GAAP Adjusted EBITDA for the second quarter 2026 was $154.6 million, an increase of 114.1% from $72.2 million for the second quarter 2025. Refer to “Non-GAAP Financial Measures” for definitions of revenue growth (excluding Bowers), Adjusted Gross Profit, Adjusted Gross Margin, Adjusted EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA Margin and a reconciliation of each to the most directly comparable GAAP measure. title: Password Statistics for 2026: Reuse, Cracks, Breaches, and the Passkey Shift
summary: Passwords are still the dominant authenticator on the internet, and they are still the thing attackers most reliably exploit.
body_text: Passwords are still the dominant authenticator on the internet, and they are still the thing attackers most reliably exploit. The Verizon 2025 Data Breach Investigations Report attributes 22% of breaches to compromised credentials as the initial access vector, and finds that 88% of basic web application attacks involved stolen credentials. Microsoft’s 2025 Digital Defense Report counted more than 7,000 password attacks per second, with 97% of identity attacks taking the form of password spray. Analysis of more than a billion malware-stolen passwords by Specops Software and Outpost24 found that 98.5% of them are weak. The figures below are the password statistics IT, security, and compliance teams should be tracking in 2026. Key password statistics at a glance 22% of breaches in 2025 used stolen credentials as the initial access vector, per the Verizon 2025 DBIR . Credentials remain the second most common entry point, just ahead of vulnerability exploitation at 20%. 1.08 billion malware-stolen passwords were captured and analyzed over a 12-month period by Specops and KrakenLabs . Of a 10-million sample, 98.5% met the modern definition of a weak password. 97% of identity attacks in 2025 were password spray attempts, and Microsoft blocked an average of more than 7,000 password attacks per second, per the Microsoft Digital Defense Report 2025 . 78% of the world’s most common passwords can be cracked in less than a second, up from 70% a year earlier, per NordPass and NordStellar . "Secret" is now the most common password in the United States. 3% of compromised passwords met basic complexity requirements in the infostealer data analyzed in the Verizon 2025 DBIR , and the median user had only 49% unique passwords across their accounts. 19% of authentication attempts to SSO providers reviewed by Verizon were credential stuffing, per the Verizon 2025 DBIR . 3 weeks is now enough to brute-force an eight-character lowercase password using twelve consumer RTX 5090 GPUs against bcrypt, per the 2025 Hive Systems Password Table . Year over year, consumer GPU cracking speed dropped cracking times by roughly 20%. 69% of online users have at least one passkey, 75% recognize the term, and 48% of the top 100 websites now support passkeys, per the FIDO Alliance . $4.44 million was the global average cost of a data breach in 2025, with credential-driven attacks remaining a core part of the story, per the IBM Cost of a Data Breach Report 2025 . ‍ Compromised credentials and the breach economy in 2026 Compromised credentials are not the only path into an enterprise, but they are still the most reliable one. The Verizon 2025 DBIR attributes 22% of breaches to stolen credentials as the initial access vector, just ahead of vulnerability exploitation at 20%. Within the basic web application attack pattern, the dependence is even more lopsided: 88% involved stolen credentials, with brute force and credential stuffing the most common tactics. The economics line up. The IBM Cost of a Data Breach Report 2025 put the global average breach cost at $4.44 million, down 9% from $4.88 million the year before, but the US average climbed to $10.22 million. IBM’s analysts have begun summarizing modern intrusion practice with the phrase "attackers are logging in, not hacking in," which is consistent with what Verizon and Microsoft are seeing on the wire. Microsoft’s 2025 Digital Defense Report adds the volumetric layer. Microsoft saw more than 7,000 password attacks per second in 2024, and 97% of all identity attacks were password spray. Out of 15.9 billion account creation requests in the first half of 2025, more than 90% came from bots, and 45% of login attempts were "valid username, wrong password," confirming how widely usernames are already exposed. The most common passwords in 2026 are still the worst ones Seven editions in, the NordPass and NordStellar Top 200 research continues to find that the world’s most common password is "123456." It has held that title in six of the last seven years. "Admin" is second globally, and the United States now has its own grim distinction: the most common password is "secret." The dataset for the 2025 edition was built from public breaches and dark-web repositories collected between September 2024 and September 2025, across 44 countries. The most striking number from the same NordPass research is that 78% of the world’s most common passwords can be cracked in less than a second, up from 70% the year before. Forty percent of the most common passwords used by individuals and by business representatives are the same, meaning the home-account problem walks straight into corporate logins. Specops’ view from the malware logs is consistent. The Specops 2025 Breached Password Report lists the top five stolen passwords as "123456," "admin," "12345678," "password," and "Password." Specops also reports that 230 million stolen passwords actually met traditional complexity requirements (eight or more characters, one capital, one number, one symbol), which is precisely why NIST has moved away from those rules. Password reuse and the credential stuffing pipeline Reuse is what turns a single breach into a wave. Infostealer infection data analyzed in the Verizon 2025 DBIR shows that in the median case only 49% of a user’s passwords are distinct from each other, meaning more than half are duplicates across services. Verizon’s same dataset found that only 3% of compromised passwords met basic complexity standards, so the typical victim is reusing weak passwords as well as a few stronger ones. That reuse fuels credential stuffing, which is now a measurable share of normal authentication traffic. The Verizon 2025 DBIR analyzed SSO provider logs and found that the median daily share of credential stuffing was 19% of all authentication attempts. In other words, on a typical day, roughly one in five login attempts to the average SSO tenant is an attacker trying credentials harvested elsewhere. Infostealers are the new password breach The credential supply chain has changed. Old-style breaches still happen, but the largest source of fresh stolen passwords today is infostealer malware running on consumer and corporate endpoints. Specops and Outpost24 captured and analyzed 1,089,342,532 stolen passwords over a single 12-month window pulled from infostealer logs, almost entirely through KrakenLabs threat intelligence. The volume continues to climb year over year. Quality is the other story. Specops analyzed a 10-million random sample from that 1-billion-plus list and found that 98.5% of the breached passwords were weak by the report’s definition (under 15 characters, or fewer than two character classes). Strong, long, complex passwords are the rare exception in the infostealer corpus, not the rule. For defenders the practical takeaway is that any password an employee has typed on an infected personal device should be considered compromised, regardless of how strong it is, how rarely it is reused, or how long the company’s rotation policy is. The Verizon 2025 DBIR specifically calls out infostealer-derived credentials as a pathway into corporate SaaS and SSO environments, since those credentials often bypass legacy network controls. How long does it actually take to crack a password in 2026 Cracking economics keep moving against defenders. The 2025 Hive Systems Password Table tested twelve RTX 5090 GPUs against bcrypt with a work factor of 10. An eight-character lowercase password fell in about three weeks. An eight-digit numeric PIN fell in 15 minutes. An eight-character password using upper case, lower case, numbers, and symbols held up far better, requiring roughly 165 years against the same rig. Year over year, consumer GPU cracking sped up by about 20%, per Hive Systems . The bigger jump came from AI accelerators. Hive’s same research found that AI-grade hardware (the kind powering large language models) accelerated cracking by more than 1.8 billion percent compared with consumer GPUs on certain workloads, collapsing what used to be a billions-of-years timeline into a few hours. The implication is that the security margin from a strong-but-short password is rapidly disappearing. This is the practical reason NIST Special Publication 800-63B (the modern federal standard for digital authentication) now treats length as the primary control. The current guidance requires a minimum of eight characters when MFA is in place and recommends or requires longer passphrases (up to 15 characters or more) for single-factor scenarios. NIST also tells systems to support at least 64 characters and to drop forced periodic rotation and composition rules, both of which it found made users pick weaker passwords. Passkey adoption and the passwordless shift Passkeys finally crossed the line from "interesting" to "default" in 2025. According to the FIDO Alliance , 75% of consumers now recognize passkeys (up from 39% in 2023), and 69% have at least one passkey set up. Forty-eight percent of the top 100 websites support passkeys, more than double the share in 2022, and the total number of accounts that can use passkeys passed 15 billion, roughly doubling year over year. The performance gap is striking. The FIDO Passkey Index reports a 93% passkey login success rate compared with 63% for traditional passwords, and a 30% conversion lift on flows that offer passkey sign-in. On the enterprise side, FIDO finds that roughly 87% of businesses have deployed or are deploying passkeys, a sharp jump from prior years. Consumer behavior is starting to follow. The FIDO Alliance reports that 54% of consumers familiar with passkeys say they are more convenient than passwords and 53% say they are more secure, while 47% of consumers abandon a purchase when they forget the password for that account. Passwords are still the dominant authenticator, but the economic case for moving away from them is now visible in the funnel data. MFA, password spray, and the limits of "just add a second factor" Multi-factor authentication blunts most credential attacks but does not eliminate them. Microsoft attributes 97% of identity attacks to password spray, which targets accounts with weak or reused passwords where the second factor is missing or weak. Less than 1% of identity attacks fall into other categories such as SIM swapping, MFA fatigue, adversary-in-the-middle phishing, and token theft, per Microsoft, but those categories are growing quickly. Microsoft reported a 146% increase in adversary-in-the-middle phishing attacks year over year. The conclusion across all three primary datasets is the same: SMS and one-time passcode MFA is increasingly bypassable, while phishing-resistant factors (FIDO2 security keys and passkeys) remain effective. The Verizon 2025 DBIR specifically flags credential stuffing as a vector that MFA enforcement reliably defeats, which is part of why MFA gaps continue to show up in the postmortems of high-impact breaches. Emerging password trends in 2026 Length is overtaking complexity in policy. The current NIST SP 800-63B guidance keeps the 8-character minimum but explicitly recommends longer passphrases and drops mandatory composition and periodic rotation rules. Specops’ finding that 230 million breached passwords met legacy complexity rules is the empirical case for the shift. Infostealer logs are now the primary stolen-password supply. A single 12-month window produced more than 1.08 billion stolen passwords per Specops . Even strong passwords typed on a compromised endpoint should be treated as burned. Passkeys cross the consumer-default threshold. At 69% of online users carrying at least one passkey and 48% of top sites supporting them ( FIDO Alliance ), passwordless authentication has moved from pilot to production for the largest consumer platforms. Credential stuffing is now a background load on every identity provider. The Verizon 2025 DBIR found that 19% of authentication attempts in observed SSO logs were credential stuffing, on a typical day. Rate limiting, anomaly detection, and impossible-travel rules are no longer optional. Workforce and consumer password habits are the same problem. NordPass found that 40% of the most common passwords used by individuals and by business representatives are identical, per NordPass . Personal credential reuse is therefore a corporate risk. AI-grade cracking changes the security margin on every offline hash. Per Hive Systems , AI accelerators have accelerated cracking by more than 1.8 billion percent versus consumer GPUs in some workloads, which means any leaked password hash is more dangerous in 2026 than it was in 2023. For broader context on the trends above, see our MFA statistics and identity theft statistics roundups. title: Blue Bird’s Vision Electric Bus Named “The Coolest Thing Made in Georgia”
summary: The Fort Valley-built bus claimed the title at the Georgia Chamber’s annual Congressional Luncheon
body_text: Macon, Ga. (August 5, 2026) – Blue Bird Corporation (Nasdaq: BLBD) walked away from the Georgia Chamber ’s annual Congressional Luncheon at The Classic Center with the title “ The Coolest Thing Made in Georgia ,” beating out a field of standout products chosen by public vote. “We’d like to thank the Georgia Chamber and all of the voters for being named ‘The Coolest Thing Made in Georgia’ for our zero-emissions electric school bus. This recognition reflects years of innovation, dedication and a shared belief that student transportation can be safer, cleaner and, yes, apparently cooler than we ever imagined,” said John Wyskiel, Blue Bird’s president and CEO. The contest ran as a social media bracket. Georgia manufacturers, makers and creators entered their products, then went head-to-head across a series of rounds. The public decided who advanced. “Public voting drove the entire contest, which makes the win land differently than an industry panel picking a favorite,” said Lauren Beaty, Blue Bird’s grants and community engagement manager. “Georgians looked at our innovative electric school bus and decided it belonged at the top.” Blue Bird is transforming the student transportation industry through cleaner energy solutions. The company is the market leader in low- and zero-emission school buses with the highest percentage of non-diesel buses sold in student transportation. As part of Georgia’s manufacturing story for close to a century, the Vision Electric bus is one of its alternative-fuel models made in Fort Valley. Blue Bird’s Vision Electric bus was named “The Coolest Thing Made in Georgia” in a statewide contest. About Blue Bird Corporation Blue Bird (NASDAQ: BLBD) is recognized as a technology leader and innovator of school buses since its founding in 1927. Our dedicated team members design, engineer and manufacture school buses with a singular focus on safety, reliability, and durability. School buses carry the most precious cargo in the world – 25 million children twice a day – making them the most trusted mode of student transportation. The company is the proven leader in low- and zero-emission school buses with more than 25,000 propane, natural gas, and electric powered buses sold. Blue Bird is transforming the student transportation industry through cleaner energy solutions. For more information on Blue Bird’s complete product and service portfolio, visit www.blue-bird.com . title: Not Just a LIMS—Your Lab’s Backbone: What Our Customers Say About Confident
summary: See why labs rely on Confident LIMS: 89% use it daily and 82% stay 1+ year. Explore compliance, integrations, and support—learn what drives trust. Learn more on Confident LIMS
body_text: Labs don’t just use Confident LIMS — they rely on it. In our 2025 lab survey, we observed that employees across labs’ entire business use Confident, that 89% of respondents reported using Confident every single day , and more than 80% have been with us for over a year. Respondents included a representative sample of Confident’s analytical testing laboratory users in the United States and Canada. Below, those survey responses are presented in precise stats to illustrate how much labs depend on Confident to run their business every day. 🎧 Prefer to listen? Here’s the audio version of this article: Who at the Lab Uses Confident LIMS? When we asked “ What role(s) do you have at your lab? ”, we saw that Confident users span across all roles at the lab — not just the core Lab Team (43%) — including Leadership (25%), Front Office (21%), Back Office (6%), and Other roles (6%) . Respondents could select multiple roles given that, reflecting how many people wear more than one hat. Pie chart showing that 43% of role selections are Lab Team, 25% Leadership, 21% Front Office, 6% Back Office, and 6% Other, illustrating that nearly every part of the lab organization relies on Confident LIMS. What this tells us: Confident isn’t a niche tool used by one department; it’s the shared system-of-record across leadership, lab operations, front office and back office teams — exactly where strategy, operations, compliance, and customer experience intersect. ‍ Daily Usage: Confident LIMS as the Operational Hub When we asked “How often do you typically use Confident?”, the results were decisive: 89% of respondents log in every day, underscoring that Confident is a daily operational system, not mission-critical tool for every day work. Pie chart showing how often users access Confident LIMS: 89% use it every day, 7% a few times per week, 2% a few times per month, and 2% rarely, highlighting that most users rely on Confident daily. With that level of daily usage, Confident effectively becomes the operational hub of the lab. If Confident isn’t available, work slows or stops. That’s why reliability, audit-ready data, and a workflow that makes sense to analysts, QA, and operations teams are so critical—and why our customers say they depend on Confident, not just “use” it. For most labs, Confident is: The system where samples are accessioned and tracked The source-of-truth for all data and calculations The source of COAs and regulatory records The platform used to communicate results to clients (often via integrated client portals) Without Confident, labs can’t operate — which is why we prioritize reliability (+99% uptime), cloud availability (work from anywhere), and fast human support (same day responses, <2 day median request-to-completion). ‍ Long-Term Relationships: Labs Stay with Confident for Years We then asked how long labs have used Confident LIMS. The answer wasn’t surprising, but it did make us proud: 82% of respondents have been on the platform for more than a year, and 40% for over three years. Pie chart showing user tenure with Confident LIMS: 11% less than six months, 7% six to twelve months, 42% one to three years, and 40% more than three years, highlighting that 82% of users have been on the platform for over a year. For a LIMS — where switching costs are high, training is intensive, and compliance is on the line — that length of tenure is a strong indicator that labs see Confident as a long-term operational partner , not a temporary tool. This aligns with broader market data: Confident LIMS is the #1 LIMS in the legal cannabis industry for 10 years in a row , trusted by 100+ labs , 15,000+ testing clients , and more than 50% of licensed cannabis labs in North America. Why Labs Depend on Confident When labs build their daily workflows around Confident, they’re betting on more than software. They’re betting on: 1. Compliance-Ready Workflows Confident LIMS supports ISO 17025, NELAP, SOC 2, and FDA 21 CFR Part 11 requirements with security and encryption, immutable audit trails, point-in-time backups, and role-based access controls. For QA leaders, that means: Every result and revision is traceable COAs are compliant, reliable, and client-ready Data is easily retrievable and always audit-ready 2. Deep Integration with Lab Equipment and Third-Party Software Systems Hundreds of labs (and thousands of their testing clients) use Confident to easily transfer data to/from their analytical instruments, regulatory systems (Metrc, BioTrack, etc), CRMs, ERPs (Quickbooks), and labeling systems — dramatically reducing manual data entry and the risk of transcription errors. This matters when: Regulations or requirements change suddenly Labs need to use data reliably and efficiently across multiple systems , not just within the LIMS 3. Client Experience that Keeps Revenue Flowing Confident’s industry-standard Client Portal and Testing Network enables customers to order tests, track their status, and securely access test results, chain of custody forms, and invoices in one place — a key reason labs stay and expand their usage over time. For lab managers and front office teams, this translates to: Fewer angry client emails and status update calls Faster turnaround on COA delivery A more modern client portal that keeps clients loyal Robust exports, analytics, and API integrations that clients demand Longer and more profitable client relationships How We Use This Survey Data At Confident, we have a simple but powerful mantra that we learned from our time at Y Combinator (S15): “Build something people want.” Easy to say. Hard to do. That’s why we didn’t conduct this survey just for a slide deck. We use the feedback to prioritize our product roadmap and support investments across the company. Here’s how user feedback like this shapes our work: High daily usage → We continually focus on performance, uptime, and an intuitive UX for busy analysts and technicians. The Best AI Alert Fatigue Reducer for Plants
summary: Alert fatigue costs plants real downtime. See how an AI alert fatigue reducer filters noise, ranks by impact, and delivers alerts your team can act on.
body_text: Key Points Alert fatigue in industrial plants happens when maintenance and operations teams face more alarms than they can act on. The ANSI/ISA-18.2 standard recommends an average alarm rate of around 6 per hour per operator, with no more than 10 in any 10-minute window. Most plants blow past those numbers, and real failures get missed inside the noise. An effective AI alert fatigue reducer filters signal at the source: it learns each asset's normal operating envelope, correlates related sensor readings into single events, ranks alerts by real business impact, and delivers a plain-language diagnosis instead of a raw threshold trip. Tractian's platform combines edge-processed vibration, temperature, and current sensors with machine learning models trained on 3.5 billion+ operational samples , driving a 43% reduction in unplanned downtime and 25% faster maintenance response time for the plants that deploy it. What Is Alert Fatigue, and Why Does It Cripple Plant Reliability? Alert fatigue is the drop in response quality and speed that happens when workers face more alarms than they can meaningfully process. On a plant floor, that looks like a technician ignoring the twentieth vibration warning of the shift, an operator muting the pressure alarm that keeps triggering during startup, or a reliability engineer who never reaches the work orders buried three pages deep in the CMMS . The problem is not carelessness. It is that legacy monitoring systems generate signal indiscriminately. Every sensor, every setpoint, every static threshold fires on its own logic without context and without ranking. The result is a firehose of notifications where important alerts sit next to trivial ones, and human attention gets rationed to whichever alarm was loudest most recently. The ANSI/ISA-18.2 standard for alarm management in the process industries lays out the target: an average annunciated alarm rate of about 6 per hour per operating position, with a maximum manageable level near 12 per hour, and no more than 10 alarms in any 10-minute window. Most plants exceed those numbers by an order of magnitude in daily operation. That is not a monitoring problem. It is a signal-to-noise problem, and it costs plants real money in missed failures, unplanned downtime, and burned-out staff. What Is an AI Alert Fatigue Reducer? An AI alert fatigue reducer is a system that uses machine learning to cut through the noise generated by traditional monitoring tools. Instead of firing every time a sensor reading crosses a static threshold, it evaluates the reading in the context of the specific asset, the current operating mode, historical patterns, and correlated signals from nearby equipment. Only when the pattern points to a real, actionable issue does it surface an alert. The best AI alert fatigue reducers do four things at once: Learn the normal operating envelope for each individual asset, not a class of assets. A conveyor motor in Plant A running at 60% load behaves differently from an identical motor in Plant B running at 90% load. Correlate signals across multiple sensors and systems. A bearing failure typically shows up as vibration change, temperature rise, and current-draw shift. A good reducer bundles those into one event, not fifteen. Rank alerts by business impact and time-to-failure . A minor imbalance on a redundant pump is not the same priority as an early cracked-race signature on a single-line critical asset. Explain the alert in language the technician can act on. Not "vibration exceeded threshold" but "outer race bearing damage detected on motor MTR-04-B, likely 2 to 4 weeks to failure, recommend replacement during the next planned shutdown." That last part is where most legacy systems fall apart. An alert without a diagnosis or a recommended action is still just noise, even if the underlying reading is accurate. Why Static Thresholds Are the Root Cause of Alert Fatigue Almost every alarm system in industrial use today runs on static thresholds. A sensor value crosses a preset number, an alert fires. This is simple to configure and easy to explain, which is why it has been the default for decades. It is also fundamentally unsuited to the reality of industrial equipment. Static thresholds ignore context. A vibration reading of 4 mm/s might be normal on a large ball mill and catastrophic on a precision grinder. The number alone does not tell you which situation you are in. Static thresholds ignore state. The same motor might run cool at idle and hot under full load, and both can be normal. A single "high temperature" alarm at 80 degrees Celsius could signal imminent failure or a routine reading during a heavy production run. Static thresholds ignore correlation. A pressure spike combined with a temperature drop and a flow change tells a specific story. A pressure spike on its own tells you almost nothing. Static thresholds ignore trend. A reading that has climbed steadily for three weeks matters far more than one that jumps and returns to normal. But the alarm fires on the number, not the trajectory. An AI alert fatigue reducer replaces these one-dimensional rules with models that learn what normal looks like for each specific machine in each specific operating condition. The alert only fires when the deviation from that learned baseline is statistically meaningful and matches a known failure mode. What Makes the Best AI Alert Fatigue Reducer for Plants Several capabilities separate a serious industrial-grade AI alert reducer from a repackaged threshold system with a machine learning label. When evaluating options, look for the following. Asset-Level Learning, Not Class-Level Assumptions Every machine is different. Two motors from the same model line, installed on the same day, in adjacent bays, will develop different vibration and thermal signatures within weeks based on load, alignment, ambient conditions, and thousands of other variables. A reducer that lumps them together as "motor" and applies the same rules will either miss failures on the tighter-tolerance machine or over-alert on the looser one. The right system builds a unique baseline for each asset and updates it continuously. Edge Processing for Real Signal Quality Vibration analysis requires high-frequency sampling, typically thousands of samples per second, to catch bearing signatures, gear mesh anomalies, and misalignment patterns. Streaming that raw data to the cloud is expensive, laggy, and unreliable on plant networks. The best systems process raw waveforms on the sensor itself and only transmit the extracted features. This gives you full-resolution analysis without saturating your network, and it means the reducer sees the real signal, not a downsampled approximation of it. Failure Mode Diagnosis, Not Just Anomaly Detection Detecting that something changed is easy. Telling the technician what changed and why is hard. A generic anomaly-detection algorithm might flag a motor as "abnormal" without indicating whether the problem is an unbalanced load, a bearing defect, misalignment, cavitation, or a loose foundation. The reducer that saves your team the most time is one that names the failure mode and prescribes the fix. Integration With the Work Order Flow An alert that lives in a separate dashboard from the CMMS is an alert that gets missed. The reducer needs to write work orders, populate them with the diagnosis, assign the right technician, order the right parts, and close the loop when the repair is complete. If the AI stops at the alert, the maintenance team still has to do all the routing work manually. That is exactly the friction that made alert fatigue a problem in the first place. Continuous Learning From Repair Outcomes Every time a technician confirms or corrects a diagnosis, the model should get better. Systems that ship a static model and never update it will slowly drift out of sync with the real behavior of the plant. Look for platforms with feedback loops that improve accuracy over time. How Tractian Reduces Alert Fatigue at the Plant Floor Level Tractian was built around this exact problem. The platform combines wireless industrial sensors for vibration, temperature, and current, edge-processed signal analysis, and machine learning models trained on 3.5 billion+ operational samples of real industrial equipment data. The alerts that reach a technician have already been filtered, correlated, and translated into a specific diagnosis with a recommended action. In practice, that means: The sensor collects high-frequency vibration and temperature data directly on the asset. Feature extraction happens at the edge, so no waveform is lost to bandwidth limits. Only meaningful signatures move to the cloud. The AI models compare those features against the learned baseline for that specific asset, against known failure signatures for that asset class, and against the current operational context. A reading that would be an alarm on one machine might be baseline noise on another, and the system knows the difference. When a deviation is real, the platform generates a diagnosis in plain language. Not "vibration anomaly detected" but "inner race bearing wear on pump P-104, estimated 3 weeks to failure." That diagnosis feeds directly into TracOS, which creates the work order, assigns a technician, and schedules the repair inside the production window. Across the plants that deploy this approach, Tractian reports a 43% reduction in unplanned downtime, a 36% reduction in parts inventory costs, and a 25% faster maintenance response time. Individual customer results have included $1M in production savings and 168 hours of avoided downtime at Ingredion, and 4 critical failures caught in the first 3 weeks of deployment at Great Plains. See the case studies here . Measurable Outcomes to Expect From a Real AI Alert Fatigue Reducer If you deploy the right platform, you should see the following categories of improvement. Alert volume per operator drops. The noise floor is filtered and correlated signals are bundled into single events, so operators see fewer notifications and each one carries more weight. Lead time on real failures expands. Instead of catching a bearing problem hours before it takes the line down, the system flags it weeks in advance, giving planning teams room to work. Unplanned downtime drops because failures get addressed inside scheduled maintenance windows instead of during production. Technician time shifts from firefighting to planned work. Wrench-time ratios improve because the team is no longer being pulled off tasks by low-value alerts. Confidence in the alarm system recovers. When teams trust that an alert means something, they respond to it. That trust is the real product of an effective reducer, and it is what makes every other benefit possible. Common Questions About AI Alert Fatigue Reducers How is an AI alert fatigue reducer different from alarm rationalization? Alarm rationalization is a manual process of reviewing and tuning existing alarms in a DCS or SCADA system. It has real value, but it happens on a project cadence (every few years) and produces static improvements. An AI alert fatigue reducer works continuously, updates itself as conditions change, and operates across multiple sources including CMMS, condition monitoring, and process control. Do we need to rip out our existing CMMS or DCS to use one? No. The best systems integrate with the tools you already run. Tractian integrates with your existing CMMS , so the AI reducer sits on top of the maintenance data layer you already have rather than forcing a rip-and-replace. How long does it take to see results? Most plants see meaningful noise reduction within 60 to 90 days of deployment, once the models have learned enough baseline data for each monitored asset. Full impact on downtime and work order quality typically shows up within two quarters. Is this only for large enterprise plants? No. AI-driven alert reduction scales down effectively because the sensors and models are per-asset rather than per-plant. A single critical line in a mid-sized facility can benefit as much as a full enterprise deployment. What happens if the AI misdiagnoses something? Every serious platform includes technician feedback loops. When a diagnosis is confirmed or corrected during a repair, the model updates. Over time, accuracy improves and the reducer becomes more tightly tuned to the specific realities of your plant. Which industries benefit most from an AI alert fatigue reducer? Any plant with rotating equipment, continuous processes, or high-consequence downtime sees strong returns. That covers food and beverage, pulp and paper, mining, cement, chemicals, oil and gas, automotive, steel, pharmaceuticals, and packaging, among others. The higher the cost of a single hour of downtime, the faster the payback. The Bottom Line Alert fatigue is not a training problem or a discipline problem. It is a system problem, caused by monitoring tools designed to detect anything rather than to detect what matters. Piling more alarms on top of an already noisy system will not fix it. Neither will asking technicians to try harder. The right AI alert fatigue reducer changes the equation. It filters noise at the source, correlates related signals, ranks by real impact, and delivers alerts a technician can act on with confidence. That is what lets a maintenance team move from reactive to proactive , and it is what turns a plant's data infrastructure into an actual competitive advantage. If your operators are drowning in alarms and your reliability team is still chasing failures after they happen, the tooling is the bottleneck. Fix that, and everything downstream gets easier. Curious to see how much of your plant's alert noise Tractian can filter out? Book a demo and we will walk through it on your own data.

body_text: BARTLETT, Tenn., Aug. 05, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- SurgePays, Inc. (NASDAQ: SURG) ("SurgePays" or the "Company"), a wireless and fintech technology company connecting subprime and underserved consumers to essential mobile and financial services, today announced the formation of Redline Wireless Group, LLC ("Redline") , a Wyoming limited liability company established as a joint venture between the Company and one of the largest wireless master distribution organizations in the United States (the "Contributing Member"), which operates an executed dealer agreement footprint of more than 20,000 active independent prepaid wireless dealers. Redline has been formed to market, distribute, and support prepaid wireless services nationwide across this independent dealer footprint. Redline will combine, in a single joint venture entity, the Company's MVNO infrastructure, including the LinkUp Mobile consumer brand, billing and provisioning systems, customer service and technical support, general and administrative infrastructure, and the Company's operations center, with access to the Contributing Member's national independent dealer prepaid wireless distribution channel. "We are pairing our full MVNO infrastructure with one of the largest independent dealer distribution footprints in the country, more than 20,000 active dealers already selling prepaid wireless every day. Our team spent over a year with LinkUp Mobile integrating and developing the systems in a live environment to support this level of scale, with the intention of building one of the largest prepaid wireless companies in the nation. Both parties share the goal of reaching more than 1 million subscribers in the coming years. Even our most conservative internal models show Redline generating more revenue and profit by month 18 than any prior SurgePays subsidiary has achieved," said Brian Cox, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of SurgePays. Redline is owned 51% by SurgePays, as controlling and managing member, and 49% by the Contributing Member (or an entity designated by the Contributing Member), as noncontrolling member. SurgePays intends to consolidate Redline as a majority-owned controlled subsidiary in accordance with Accounting Standards Codification 810, with the Contributing Member's 49% economic interest reported as a noncontrolling interest. body_text: Home » Newsroom » Blog » TechRadar: Data movement is the new performance battleground in semiconductor design TechRadar: Data movement is the new performance battleground in semiconductor design Aug 11, 2026 Andy Nightingale < 1 min read For much of the semiconductor industry’s history, performance debates have centered on compute throughput and memory capacity. Faster processors, wider vectors, and larger caches have been the primary levers for system architects, often treating the movement of data between them as a secondary concern. Today, a different constraint is asserting itself as AI data center workloads proliferate, architectures diversify, and systems extend beyond traditional computing into the physical world. Data movement, rather than processing or storage, is increasingly defining the limits of performance, power efficiency, predictability, determinism, and scalability. This shift around data movement is already visible. Across applications like advanced SoCs, AI accelerators, chiplet-based systems, and now in physical AI applications such as robotics, industrial automation, and intelligent vehicles, it has become clear that transporting the vast quantities of data required by such workloads is more demanding than processing them. Physical AI does not introduce a new problem so much as it exposes an existing one: when systems must perceive, decide, and act in closed loops under real-time and safety constraints, inefficient or unpredictable data movement quickly becomes the dominant bottleneck.
