title: Why Your DOOH Ads Need Better Audience Segmentation
summary: Digital out-of-home advertising is growing fast, but many campaigns still rely on broad demographic assumptions rather than precise audience intelligence.
body_text: Digital out-of-home advertising is growing fast, but many campaigns still rely on broad demographic assumptions rather than precise audience intelligence. Improving your DOOH audience segmentation strategy can transform campaign performance by reaching the right people at the right moments. This guide covers how segmentation works, why it matters, and how to implement it effectively across your campaigns. Key Takeaways Q: Why does DOOH audience segmentation outperform broad demographic targeting? A: It replaces guesswork with data-informed decisions, matching screen activations to the audiences most likely present at a given time and place—reducing wasted impressions and improving return on ad spend. Q: How does audience-first planning uncover high-performing DOOH inventory? A: By starting with movement data for a defined audience rather than selecting premium locations, advertisers often discover niche screens—such as those near daycare centers or clinics—with higher target-audience concentration than busy malls. Q: What role does points of interest targeting play in DOOH audience segmentation? A: It activates ads near contextually relevant real-world locations (competitor stores, gyms, transit hubs), reaching people at moments when their intent or mindset aligns with the advertised product. Q: How can advertisers measure whether their segmented DOOH campaigns actually work? A: Mobile-based attribution links anonymized device exposure near activated screens to downstream actions like store visits or purchases, while brand lift studies reveal which audience segments responded most strongly. Q: What makes contextual targeting a privacy-safe complement to audience-based DOOH segmentation? A: It relies on environmental signals—weather, time of day, venue type—rather than personal data, delivering relevant messaging without individual-level tracking while still maintaining targeting precision. Q: How does Perion support granular DOOH audience segmentation for programmatic campaigns? A: Perion’s platform integrates location intelligence, behavioral data, and contextual signals so advertisers can build, activate, and measure precise audience segments across programmatic DOOH inventory within a single ecosystem. Q: What is the recommended starting point for brands launching their first segmented DOOH campaign? A: Begin with two to three well-defined audience segments, map inventory using audience indexing data, develop segment-specific creative, and optimize weekly based on performance—keeping the scope focused for clearer measurement. What Is DOOH Audience Segmentation, Exactly? DOOH audience segmentation is the practice of dividing potential viewers of digital out-of-home ads into distinct groups based on shared characteristics, behaviors, or contextual signals. Rather than treating every person who passes a billboard as an identical prospect, segmentation allows advertisers to tailor messaging, timing, and placement to specific audience clusters. Key Dimensions of Segmentation Audience segments in DOOH can be built across multiple dimensions. Understanding these dimensions helps advertisers select the right combination for their campaign goals. Demographic: Age, gender, income level, household composition, and education level derived from census data and mobile panel insights. Behavioral: Purchase history, app usage patterns, media consumption habits, and brand affinity signals collected from opted-in mobile data. Contextual: Weather conditions, time of day, day of week, nearby events, and seasonal trends that influence receptivity to specific messages. Geographic: Hyper-local targeting based on neighborhoods, transit corridors, retail zones, and commuter patterns. How It Differs from Traditional OOH Targeting Traditional out-of-home advertising relied almost entirely on location selection and estimated traffic counts. Advertisers chose a billboard on a busy highway and hoped the right people drove past it. DOOH audience segmentation replaces that guesswork with data-informed decisions, matching screen activations to the audiences most likely to be present at a given time and place. This shift makes DOOH measurable and accountable in ways that static OOH never could be. Why Precision Targeting Is Essential for Modern DOOH Campaigns Precision targeting has moved from a competitive advantage to a baseline expectation for media buyers. Brands allocating budget to DOOH expect the same level of audience accountability they receive from digital display, connected TV, and social channels. The Cost of Broad Targeting When campaigns target everyone, they effectively target no one with meaningful impact. Broad targeting leads to several measurable problems: Wasted impressions served to audiences with zero purchase intent for the advertised product. Diluted creative impact because generic messaging fails to resonate with any specific group. Difficulty attributing outcomes, since broad campaigns lack the audience definition needed for meaningful lift studies. Reduced budget efficiency, as CPMs are spent reaching irrelevant viewers instead of high-value prospects. What Precision Targeting Delivers By contrast, precision targeting allows advertisers to activate screens only when and where their defined audience is most concentrated. A quick-service restaurant chain, for example, can target screens near office complexes during the lunch hour when foot traffic from working professionals peaks. A luxury automotive brand can focus on affluent commuter corridors during weekday mornings. The result is higher relevance per impression and stronger return on ad spend. Platforms like Perion’s programmatic DOOH solutions enable this level of precision by combining mobile location data, audience indexing, and real-time bidding to activate the right screens at the right moments. This approach brings digital-grade targeting to physical-world advertising. A Look at How DOOH Audience Segmentation Works in Practice Understanding how DOOH audience segmentation works requires looking at the data pipeline from audience definition through screen activation and measurement. The process involves several interconnected steps that turn raw data into actionable campaign decisions. Step 1: Define the Target Audience Advertisers begin by specifying who they want to reach. This definition can come from first-party CRM data, third-party audience segments, or custom behavioral profiles. For instance, a fitness brand might define its audience as health-conscious adults aged 25 to 44 who frequent gyms and purchase organic groceries. Step 2: Map Audience Movement Patterns Using anonymized and aggregated mobile device data, platforms analyze where the defined audience spends time throughout the day. This creates a movement map showing concentration patterns across different locations, times, and days of the week. Step 3: Match Audiences to Screen Inventory The movement data is then overlaid against available DOOH screen inventory. Screens are scored based on how strongly they index against the target audience compared to the general population. A screen near a university campus might index highly for Gen Z consumers but poorly for retirees. Step 4: Activate and Optimize Campaigns are activated programmatically, with bids placed on screen inventory that meets minimum audience composition thresholds. Throughout the campaign, performance data feeds back into the system to shift spend toward the highest-performing screens and dayparts. Stage Primary Data Source Output Audience Definition CRM, third-party segments, behavioral panels Target audience profile Movement Mapping Anonymized mobile location data Location and time heatmaps Screen Matching SSP inventory feeds, audience indices Ranked screen list with audience scores Activation and Optimization Real-time bidding signals, impression logs Optimized media delivery Shifting to an Audience-Driven Targeting Strategy Many advertisers still plan DOOH campaigns by selecting locations first and audiences second. An audience-driven targeting approach reverses that order, starting with the people you want to reach and then identifying where they are most likely to encounter your message. Location-First vs. Audience-First Planning The difference between these two approaches is significant in both process and outcome. Location-first: The advertiser selects a set of screens in premium locations (airports, malls, highway billboards) and assumes the right people will see the ads. This approach prioritizes visibility over relevance. Audience-first: The advertiser defines a target audience, analyzes movement data, and selects screens based on audience concentration. This approach prioritizes relevance and may surface unexpected, high-performing locations. Why Audience-Driven Targeting Produces Better Results Audience-driven targeting often reveals screen inventory that location-first planners would overlook. A campaign targeting young parents, for example, might discover that screens near pediatric clinics and daycare centers outperform screens in high-traffic shopping malls. The audience composition at those niche locations is far more concentrated, even if total foot traffic is lower. Perion supports audience-driven targeting through its advertising platform, which allows buyers to build campaigns around audience segments rather than static venue lists. This flexibility helps brands discover efficient inventory and reduce wasted spend. Making the Organizational Shift Transitioning to audience-driven targeting requires changes beyond technology. Media planning teams need access to audience data tools, creative teams need to develop segment-specific messaging, and measurement frameworks need to evaluate campaigns based on audience reach rather than screen count alone. Brands that make this shift consistently report improved campaign efficiency and stronger attribution outcomes. Using Points of Interest Targeting to Reach People in Key Moments Points of interest targeting is a segmentation tactic that activates DOOH ads based on proximity to specific real-world locations. These locations, known as points of interest (POIs), serve as behavioral proxies that indicate audience intent, lifestyle, or immediate needs. What Qualifies as a Point of Interest POIs can include virtually any physical location that carries behavioral significance for a brand’s target audience. Common categories include: Retail locations: Competitor stores, complementary retailers, category-specific shops. Lifestyle venues: Gyms, spas, restaurants, entertainment venues, sports stadiums. Transit hubs: Train stations, bus stops, airports, ride-share pickup zones. Healthcare facilities: Hospitals, pharmacies, dental offices, wellness clinics. Educational institutions: Universities, trade schools, tutoring centers. Contextual Relevance at the Moment of Exposure The power of points of interest targeting lies in contextual alignment. A sunscreen brand advertising on screens near beach access points reaches people at the exact moment they are thinking about sun protection. A financial services company targeting screens near auto dealerships reaches consumers who may be actively considering financing options. This contextual relevance dramatically increases the likelihood that an ad will register and influence behavior. Combining POI Targeting with Audience Data The most effective campaigns layer POI targeting with audience segmentation. Instead of targeting all screens near gyms, a sports nutrition brand can target screens near gyms only during hours when its core demographic (males aged 18 to 34) is most likely to be present. This layered approach combines the contextual power of location with the precision of audience data. Core Methods for Accurate DOOH Audience Measurement Effective DOOH audience measurement answers a fundamental question: did the right people actually see the ad, and did it change their behavior? Measurement in DOOH has advanced significantly, moving beyond estimated impressions to include verified exposure and outcome-based metrics. Impression Measurement Frameworks Several industry bodies have established standards for counting DOOH impressions. The most widely adopted frameworks include: Framework Organization Methodology EYES ON Geopath (U.S.) Combines traffic counts, eye-tracking studies, and visibility adjustments to estimate likely-to-see impressions Route Route Research (U.K.) Uses GPS tracking panels and travel survey data to model audience exposure across OOH formats COMMB Canadian OOH Marketing Bureau Integrates mobile data with traffic studies to produce audience reach and frequency estimates Mobile-Based Attribution Mobile device data has become a primary tool for DOOH audience measurement. By analyzing anonymized device IDs observed near activated screens, advertisers can determine whether exposed audiences subsequently visited a store, downloaded an app, or made a purchase. This exposure-to-outcome chain provides attribution data that was previously unavailable for out-of-home media. Brand Lift Studies Brand lift measurement compares survey responses from audiences exposed to DOOH ads against a control group that was not exposed. These studies measure changes in awareness, consideration, favorability, and purchase intent. When combined with audience segmentation data, brand lift studies can reveal which segments responded most strongly to the campaign, informing future targeting decisions. Cross-Channel Measurement Advanced measurement approaches track how DOOH exposure influences behavior across other channels. For example, did people who saw a DOOH ad later search for the brand on Google, visit the brand’s website, or engage with a social media post? Perion’s cross-channel capabilities help advertisers connect DOOH exposure to downstream digital actions, providing a more complete picture of campaign impact. Inspiring Real-World Applications from Top Brands in 2026 The most compelling evidence for DOOH audience segmentation comes from brands that have implemented it successfully. These real-world applications demonstrate how segmentation translates from theory into measurable business outcomes. Quick-Service Restaurants: Daypart and Demographic Targeting Major QSR chains have adopted DOOH segmentation to promote different menu items to different audiences throughout the day. Breakfast items are served on screens near commuter routes during morning hours when working professionals are most concentrated. Late-night snack promotions activate on screens near entertainment districts when younger demographics are present. This daypart-plus-demographic approach has allowed QSR brands to increase menu-specific sales lift compared to static, always-on campaigns. Automotive: Conquest Targeting Near Competitor Dealerships Automotive brands have used points of interest targeting to serve ads on DOOH screens near competitor dealerships. By targeting screens within a defined radius of rival showrooms and filtering for audiences in the market for a new vehicle, these campaigns reach consumers at a high-intent moment. Several brands have reported measurable increases in dealership visit rates among exposed audiences. Retail and CPG: Weather-Triggered Segmentation Consumer packaged goods brands have combined audience segmentation with weather data to trigger contextually relevant creative. A beverage company, for example, can activate cold drink promotions on screens in areas where temperatures exceed a set threshold and where its target demographic is concentrated. This combination of environmental context and audience data produces campaigns that feel timely and personally relevant. Travel and Tourism: Seasonal Audience Shifts Tourism boards and travel brands use segmentation to adjust messaging based on seasonal audience composition. Screens in ski resort towns receive different creative during peak season (targeting visiting tourists) versus off-season (targeting local residents with summer activity promotions). Audience data ensures that the right message reaches the right population mix at each time of year. Finding the Right Data Partners for Granular Segmentation The quality of DOOH audience segmentation depends directly on the quality of underlying data. Selecting the right data partners is a critical decision that affects targeting accuracy, measurement reliability, and regulatory compliance. What to Evaluate in a Data Partner Not all audience data providers offer the same level of quality or coverage. Advertisers should assess potential partners across several criteria: Panel size and representativeness: Larger, more diverse panels produce more accurate audience models. Ask about panel composition across age, income, ethnicity, and geography. Data freshness: Audience movement patterns change. Partners should update their data frequently enough to reflect current behaviors rather than outdated patterns. Privacy compliance: Partners must adhere to applicable regulations such as GDPR, CCPA, and other regional privacy laws. Data should be anonymized and aggregated, with clear consent mechanisms in place. Integration capabilities: The data must integrate smoothly with your DSP or programmatic buying platform. Proprietary formats or siloed data sets create friction and reduce campaign agility. First-Party, Second-Party, and Third-Party Data The strongest segmentation strategies combine multiple data types. First-party data from a brand’s own CRM or loyalty program provides high-fidelity audience definitions. Second-party data from trusted partners (such as a retailer sharing purchase data with a CPG brand) adds behavioral depth. Third-party data from audience data providers offers scale and reach across broader population segments. Perion’s Approach to Data-Driven DOOH Perion integrates multiple data sources within its advertising platform to support granular DOOH audience segmentation. By combining location intelligence, behavioral data, and contextual signals, Perion enables advertisers to build and activate precise audience segments across programmatic DOOH inventory. This integrated approach reduces the need for advertisers to manage multiple vendor relationships for data, activation, and measurement. The Future of Segmentation: Privacy and Personalization DOOH audience segmentation is advancing alongside broader shifts in data privacy regulation and consumer expectations. Advertisers must balance the desire for granular targeting with the responsibility to respect individual privacy. Privacy-Compliant Segmentation Models The most sustainable segmentation approaches rely on aggregated and anonymized data rather than individual-level tracking. Key principles for privacy-compliant DOOH targeting include: Using cohort-based models that group users into segments without identifying individuals. Ensuring all mobile location data comes from opted-in sources with transparent consent mechanisms. Applying differential privacy techniques that add statistical noise to prevent re-identification of individuals within data sets. Complying with all applicable regulations and proactively adapting to new legislation as it emerges. Contextual Intelligence as a Privacy-Safe Alternative Contextual targeting offers a powerful complement to audience-based approaches, particularly in privacy-sensitive environments. By analyzing environmental signals such as weather, time of day, nearby events, and venue type, advertisers can deliver relevant messaging without relying on personal data. A screen in a shopping mall food court during lunchtime carries strong contextual signals about the audience’s mindset and needs, regardless of who specifically is present. The Personalization Spectrum DOOH will never offer the one-to-one personalization of a mobile ad served to a single device. Instead, DOOH operates on a spectrum of personalization, from broad demographic targeting to highly specific segment-plus-context combinations. The most effective campaigns find the point on this spectrum where relevance is maximized without overstepping privacy boundaries. As measurement technology improves and privacy frameworks mature, this balance point will continue to shift toward greater precision. Steps to Launch Your First Segmented DOOH Campaign For advertisers ready to move beyond broad DOOH buys, launching a segmented campaign requires a structured approach. The following steps provide a practical framework for getting started. Step 1: Clarify Campaign Objectives Define what success looks like before selecting audience segments. Are you driving foot traffic to retail locations? Building brand awareness among a new demographic? Conquesting competitor customers? Your objective determines which segments matter most and how you will measure results. Step 2: Build Your Audience Segments Work with your data partners or platform provider to construct audience segments aligned with your objectives. Start with two to three well-defined segments rather than attempting to target dozens of micro-segments simultaneously. This focused approach makes it easier to evaluate performance and iterate. Step 3: Select Inventory and Dayparts Use audience indexing data to identify which screens and time slots deliver the highest concentration of your target segments. Prioritize inventory where your audience index significantly exceeds the general population baseline. Step 4: Develop Segment-Specific Creative Create ad variations tailored to each segment’s motivations and context. A campaign targeting commuters during morning rush hour should use different messaging than one targeting weekend shoppers. Even small creative adjustments, such as changing a headline or call to action, can significantly improve resonance. Step 5: Activate, Measure, and Optimize Launch the campaign through a programmatic DOOH platform that supports audience-based buying. Establish measurement baselines during the first week, then optimize by shifting budget toward the segments, screens, and dayparts that deliver the strongest results. Platforms like Perion provide the activation and measurement infrastructure needed to execute this optimization cycle efficiently. A Quick-Reference Checklist Objective defined: Clear, measurable goal tied to business outcomes. Segments built: Two to three audience segments with data-backed definitions. Inventory mapped: Screens selected based on audience composition, not just traffic volume. Creative developed: At least one creative variation per segment. Measurement plan set: KPIs, attribution methodology, and reporting cadence established before launch. Optimization schedule: Weekly review points to reallocate budget based on performance data. DOOH audience segmentation is no longer optional for advertisers who expect measurable outcomes from their out-of-home investments. By combining audience intelligence, contextual signals, and programmatic activation, brands can transform DOOH from a broad awareness channel into a precision marketing tool that delivers accountable results at every stage of the funnel. title: Same Expertise, Different Wrapper: CHDG Builds on Dynamic Hedging Legacy
summary: Calamos Active Hedged Equity ETF’s dynamic hedging approach is designed to capitalize on changing markets and volatility in ways that static approaches can’t. Senior Co-Portfolio Manager Dave O’Donohue speaks to the advantages that CHDG brings.
body_text: Same Expertise, Different Wrapper: CHDG Builds on Dynamic Hedging Legacy August 4, 2026 Calamos Investments continues its rapid-fire innovation in the ETF space with the launch of Calamos Active Hedged Equity ETF (CHDG) . Launched on August 4, CHDG builds on the firm’s pioneering experience in risk-managed alternatives—including dynamic hedging. We sat down with Dave O’Donohue, Co-Head of Alternative Strategies and Senior Co-Portfolio Manager, to find out more about the fund and what makes it stand out. Q. Dave, what’s CHDG designed to do? A. CHDG is trying to give investors equity market participation and a meaningful total return but with less downside risk and lower volatility than full equity exposure. Q. Is hedged equity a new strategy for Calamos? A. CHDG is our first hedged equity strategy in an ETF wrapper, but using options to hedge equity risk has been part of Calamos since day one. In fact, our Global CIO John Calamos, Sr., was using options even before he founded Calamos Investments in the 1970s. More recently, our team has been running a very similar strategy in our open-end Calamos Hedged Equity Fund (CIHEX) for almost 12 years now, and a slightly different octane version in our Calamos Market Neutral Income Fund (CMNIX) for over 20 years. Combined, those two funds have over $19 billion in assets and over $10 billion dedicated to hedged equity, so we have been running hedged equity strategies at large scale for decades—but now it’s available in the ETF wrapper that many have asked for. Q. There are a lot of hedged equity strategies in the market. What do you bring to the table that’s different? A. Most of the hedged equity strategies available today are very systematic. They use the same hedge every time and simply roll it once a quarter or once a month. While that might be simple to execute and explain, we just philosophically don’t believe that’s the right approach for investors. Quite frankly, there isn’t just one hedge structure that always works best. If there were, everyone would do it. Realistically, markets change over time—volatility changes over time. There will be periods when buying puts is really attractive, times when selling calls is really attractive, and times when both are challenging. Instead of forcing our way into a predetermined hedge, we’d rather step back and ask ourselves, what’s unique about this market, and what opportunity does that present for us? What’s easier to do, and what’s more challenging? There are a lot of different ways to get hedged, and it’s our job to understand what's best given today’s environment. Q. With your active approach, how often is the hedge adjusted? A. It really depends on the market. We think of our hedge as being a living, breathing hedge—we adjust it continually so we try to use market volatility to our advantage. While most of the hedge will be largely set, we are always looking for adjustments we could add today that might not have been available before. If the market is up 2% one day, we’re thinking about whether we can sell another call or roll up a put strike, or even add in another put for less than we could yesterday or a week ago. If the market falls, can we cover a call we wrote or perhaps monetize some extra puts we bought? If you think about it like a shopping list, if I have to buy exactly what’s on that list and all in one day, I’m simply at the mercy of prices that day. If I have a little flexibility though, to buy what’s on sale that day, I can finish out that list much more cheaply. Hedging is no different. I'm far better off if I can stock up on puts when prices are low than if I have to add them when markets are falling and volatility is high and you have the option equivalent of "surge pricing." By adjusting the hedge to structures that fit the current environment, and also by adding in those pieces opportunistically along the way, we think we can create a more efficient hedge over time than we would be able to on any one set day—and certainly on one day with a predetermined structure. Q. How would you sum up the benefits of your active approach? A. We believe shaping the hedge to market conditions plus active management along the way can do two important things: first, we can create a more efficient hedge that leads to better returns, and second, we can create a smoother ride—without the risk of massive deviations. For a lot of systematic approaches, the beta can change intra-quarter and around every reset. So, at certain times, these approaches have a lot of equity sensitivity and other times very little. Maybe that equals out to a 0.5 to 0.6 beta over time, but it certainly may not. That’s been the case recently. Our approach focuses on maintaining a consistent profile over time, which we believe delivers a smoother ride that investors are hoping for. Q. What does CHDG’s hedge look like now? A. Right now is a great example of the power of being able to shape our hedge to best take advantage of market conditions. Current interest rates and volatility levels give us a fairly unusual opportunity to structure CHDG’s payout profile to aim to capture 65% or so of the market upside, with only 35% or so of the downside. This type of asymmetry just wasn’t possible for most of the last 25 years and certainly wasn’t an option for us when we launched our hedged equity mutual fund or when many of the systematic funds were launched. Because of our flexibility though, when this did become available, we were able to adjust and implement it in our hedged equity mutual fund, and again here with CHDG. We think this 65/35 profile fits really well with what our core investors are hoping for from hedged equity. When you find opportunities like this that fit so well with what your investors want, our main focus now is to lock the hedge in with as much certainty and predictability as possible and for as long as possible. Thanks, Dave. Any final thoughts? Our team has a long history of working together on Calamos Market Neutral Income Fund and Calamos Hedged Equity Fund. And of course, Calamos Investments has always been at the forefront of alternatives. We’re excited for the opportunity to bring what we believe is a best-in-class hedged equity strategy to ETF investors. CHDG Advantages There is no guarantee these objectives will be achieved. title: Daré Bioscience Announces Pricing of $6.0 Million Registered Direct Offering Priced At-The-Market Under Nasdaq Rules

body_text: SAN DIEGO, Aug. 14, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Daré Bioscience, Inc. (Nasdaq: DARE), a purpose-driven health biotech company solely focused on closing the gap in women’s health between promising science and real-world solutions, today announced that it has entered into a definitive securities purchase agreement with institutional investors for the purchase and sale of 4,379,581 shares of the Company’s common stock (or pre-funded warrants to purchase shares of common stock in lieu thereof), at a price of $1.37 per share of common stock (or $1.3699 per pre-funded warrant) in a registered direct offering priced at-the-market under Nasdaq rules. Each pre-funded warrant will be exercisable upon issuance at an exercise price of $0.0001 per share and will expire when exercised in full. In addition, in a concurrent private placement, the Company will issue to the investors Series A warrants to purchase in the aggregate up to 4,379,581 shares of common stock, and Series B warrants to purchase in the aggregate up to 4,379,581 shares of common stock (or pre-funded warrants to purchase shares of common stock in lieu thereof). The exercisability of both the Series A warrants and the Series B warrants will be subject to obtaining stockholder approval as may be required under Nasdaq rules. The Series A warrants will have an exercise price of $1.37 per share, will be exercisable on or after stockholder approval, and will have a term of five years from the initial exercise date. The Series B warrants will have an exercise price of $1.37 per share, will be exercisable on or after stockholder approval, and will have a term of two years from the initial exercise date. The aggregate gross proceeds to the Company from the registered direct offering at the closing are expected to be $6.0 million before deducting placement agent fees and estimated offering expenses payable by the Company. title: Stripe agrees to acquire OpenRouter to help businesses optimize token routing and usage
summary: Stripe, the programmable financial services company, today announced that it has agreed to acquire OpenRouter, a leading AI model gateway and routing platform.
body_text: SAN FRANCISCO AND DUBLIN—Stripe, the programmable financial services company, today announced that it has agreed to acquire OpenRouter, a leading AI model gateway and routing platform. OpenRouter helps businesses route and optimize token usage across 400+ models from more than 80 providers. Stripe provides economic infrastructure for the world’s fastest-growing businesses, including the vast majority of companies developing and building with AI. Stripe already helps businesses maximize their revenue by optimizing across a complex set of variables like payment methods, authorization rates, and fraud. Since last year, Stripe has also worked to help companies optimize their token costs and route tokens efficiently, launching products like Token Billing. But token optimization is about more than just costs. The sheer matrix of variables—which model to use for which tasks, at which speed and at what price—makes managing cost-versus-performance tradeoffs in real time extremely difficult. This challenge is exacerbated by the pace at which models are released and repriced. OpenRouter has built a platform that helps businesses dynamically evaluate each request, routing it to the optimal model based on task complexity, price, speed, and reliability, and is already used by the likes of NVIDIA, Zoom, and Lovable. Together, Stripe and OpenRouter will be able to help companies manage both sides of profitability in the AI era: maximizing revenue and efficacy while minimizing costs. “Tokens are the central currency for companies building with AI, and it’s clear that the real-world economic potential will depend on making good use of scarce compute resources,” said Patrick Collison, cofounder and CEO of Stripe. “Stripe is building the economic infrastructure for AI, and together with OpenRouter we’ll help businesses maximize profitability by routing their requests intelligently and spending their tokens efficiently.” “Stripe has spent over a decade building trusted, neutral infrastructure for businesses, and OpenRouter was built on the same philosophy,” said Alex Atallah, cofounder and CEO of OpenRouter. “We believe intelligence will be multi-model: no single model will be optimal for every task, and developers need a neutral layer to orchestrate and manage them all. Joining Stripe lets us accelerate that mission and bring the full AI ecosystem to every business.”

title: What it takes to hold and maintain forestry certifications
summary: What it takes to hold and maintain forestry certifications
body_text: All the forestlands we own are certified by the FSC and/or the PEFC, and all the fiber we harvest or purchase from others is chain-of-custody certified. But what does that mean in terms of how we do business and what we produce? There are many requirements our forestry teams have to fulfill for us to maintain these certifications. Each have their own criteria to evaluate whether we are successfully practicing sustainable forestry, but they do have similarities. While not an exhaustive list, here are some basic requirements for maintaining these certifications, categorized by the three pillars of sustainable forest management: environmental, economic and social. There are many requirements our forestry teams have to fulfill for us to maintain these certifications. Each have their own criteria to evaluate whether we are successfully practicing sustainable forestry, but they do have similarities. While not an exhaustive list, here are some basic requirements for maintaining these certifications, categorized by the three pillars of sustainable forest management: environmental, economic and social. Environmental Requirements Since the 90s, there are many environmental laws now in effect globally. These laws concern endangered species, waste handling, logging, water usage and the treatment of wetlands, as well as soil conservation practices. Recognizing them, certification organizations always require adherence to all applicable laws in their region. In addition to complying with applicable laws, foresters must show they are abiding by sustainable forestry practices in specific ways: Developing and Filing Management Plans Certification bodies require foresters to file forest management plans that are also made available to the public. The plans must have goals based on how the land will be used, and they must be assessed against these goals, revised and updated periodically. The management plan must include mapping of the forest region under the plan, and it also must document all planned activities for that region, including but not limited to: Research Assessments Any harvesting or thinning according to best practices Pest control Soil supplementation Support of endangered species Communication with the surrounding community Foreseeable mitigation efforts When developing and revising management plans, foresters work with regional organizations to evaluate the best ways to manage forest health while also continuing to provide the forest products on which the world relies. This long-term planning promotes biodiversity and prevents deforestation since its aim is to keep forests productive and healthy today and into the future. “We may work with outside organizations like the National Council for Air and Stream Improvement (NCASI) to analyze forest growth at a landscape level to make sure we have a sustainable fiber supply,” said Eric Smith, Smurfit Westrock senior manager of sustainability for North America, who creates sustainable forest management plans for private landowners. “As a part of the management plan for our forests in Brazil, for example, we preserve 0.8 of a hectare of natural forest for every hectare we plant,” said Heuzer Guimaraes, Smurfit Westrock VP of fiber and forestry for Brazil. Active Monitoring and Maintaining of Forest Health According to Plans Once a management plan is accepted, it has to be carried out. Through ongoing forest management operations, foresters maintain and support biodiversity and forest health because forests are necessary for maintaining sustainability, productivity, and the sequestration of carbon in the atmosphere. This includes protecting the flora and fauna as well as the integrity of the soil and water resources. Periodic audits and surveys of the land help foresters monitor and assess forest conditions. They look for things like evidence of disease, problems with pests, or evidence of water erosion. Foresters must also record certain high conservation values to show health is being maintained or improving. For example, they document native species, the variety of species and if there are rare or threatened habitats. As forests are monitored over time, numbers and information can be compared to previous years. Through this thorough auditing and documentation, foresters then evaluate whether the management plan is successful and recommend mitigation activities and revisions if necessary. One issue foresters may need to address is pests that reduce forest productivity. However, certification bodies require that foresters show how they are minimizing the use of products like insecticides. “We must show the ways we are controlling insects, even if we are developing biological treatments instead of using chemicals,” said Guimaraes. “For example, for most insects, we introduce a natural predator to control the species that is creating the problem on our plantation.” In order to maintain certification, foresters are only allowed to introduce a non-native species if there is scientific support showing it would be beneficial to the habitat. Working to Improve Forest Health To uphold certifications, foresters must prevent damage to the ecosystem and implement mitigation plans if needed. For example, if there is any erosion caused by harvesting, if there’s any damage to roads or if there’s any impact to soil or water quality, foresters restore what was impacted. “A harvest is one of the most critical points, because there can be some erosion to the soil that can impact the watershed,” said Marcela Zapata, Smurfit Westrock head of forestry research and development in Colombia . “So, we have to provide evidence that we are mitigating that impact after the harvest. Transporting the wood is another activity that can result in the need for mitigation.” In addition to mitigation, our experts focus on other areas of forest health. Whenever necessary and feasible, they must design and implement sustainable strategies for the prevention, control, and integrated management of pests and diseases, a high priority of our Forest Health Program. For example, when disease or fungi affect plants and trees, foresters must address it so it doesn’t spread. Foresters must also work with environmental organizations to improve habitats to support the return of endangered species. For the forest plantations we own, it’s most important for foresters to balance sustainability and forest health with productivity. Sustainable forestry practices in combination with planting with high-quality material have contributed to enhanced productivity among diverse and challenging environmental conditions. Social Requirements The reason forest management plans are made public is because there is always an expectation that foresters will be in regular communication with the community surrounding the forests they manage. Certification bodies require communication regarding how forestry operations may impact the community, especially when it comes to roads, infrastructure or the environment. Businesses involved in forestry must also abide by fair labor and equal employment practices, focusing on providing a living wage and employing all peoples regardless of gender, race, ethnicity or sexuality. Safety is also a major concern, so providing adequate training, tools and equipment is critical. “We have to provide the right tools and equipment for protection, such as helmets, gloves and masks,” said Zapata. “Safety is not just a requirement; it’s a priority here, and it’s important to train people to have a safety-first mindset.” With regard to the community, work with indigenous peoples is specifically addressed by certification bodies. Foresters must recognize not only the customs and traditions of the indigenous, but also their rights to ownership and use of the forestland and its resources. Economic Requirements Since sustainable forestry acknowledges the need for economic benefit, certification bodies require that foresters show that the community, as well as the company, is benefitting from forestry activities. Companies must pay foresters wages that meet or exceed the standard in the industry. They must also seek to use local vendors when securing third-party resources for their activities and must show their management plans are viable for the economy over the long term. Our foresters say that, overall, they must always be thinking about how they can positively impact the local community. “We provide for the local economy through the amount of scholarship support we have developed with universities and research support. There are also social programs we developed in our region to educate and inform,” said Guimaraes. Going beyond forestry to maintain an ethical supply chain While these certifications are important to the forests we own, we also secure fiber from others. To show that fiber comes from sustainably managed forests, we secure chain-of-custody certifications. “Before we move a logger onto a site, we're doing many of the same things on the non-certified lands we don’t own, that we're doing on our own certified lands. That’s essential to our responsible fiber sourcing certifications,” said Smith. “While we’re not able to claim fiber from those lands is certified, we still have a responsibility to make sure we have a sustainable fiber supply now and into the future.” We have team members who’ve served in working groups to update the FSC and SFI standards. Most recently this included participating in FSC International’s core working group to help update and improve chain-of-custody standards. Through giving the working group tours of two of our mills in Germany, those involved were able to see chain of custody standards in practice as recycled paper was turned into packaging. Seeing practical application of its standards in the industry is an important step to ensuring those standards continue to be meaningful. Certifications from the FSC and PEFC help people to know how a business is managing their forestlands and protecting the environment, while SFI responsible fiber sourcing certifications show that the fiber sourced from non-certified lands is also sustainably managed. These certifications give producers, brands and consumers peace of mind in knowing their packaging is not contributing to deforestation or toward harming ecosystems. View our most recent Sustainability Report for more information. View Sustainability Report

title: Petty Cash Accounting: How to Set Up, Track, and Reconcile Petty Cash Fund
summary: Petty cash accounting explained how to set up an imprest fund, record disbursements, replenish fund, and reconcile at month-end. Journal entries, controls, and common mistakes.
body_text: Petty cash is a small amount of physical currency a business keeps on hand for minor expenses too small to justify writing a check or using a corporate card postage stamps, office supplies runs, employee lunch reimbursements, small vendor payments. The accounting mechanic is imprest fund total should always equal original petty cash amount, made up partly of cash and partly of receipts documenting disbursements. This guide walks through setup, journal entries, replenishment, reconciliation, and common mistakes. Per Investopedia's petty cash explainer , imprest system is standard practice because it makes reconciliation simple: cash + receipts should always equal fund's original balance. Setting up petty cash fund Two decisions at setup: How much? Most small businesses run a petty cash fund of $100–$500 . Larger businesses with heavy in-office petty spending might run $1,000. Too little means constant replenishment; too much creates unnecessary loss and security exposure. Who's custodian? One person is designated to manage fund. That person keeps cash physically secure, records disbursements on a petty cash log, and requests replenishment when fund runs low. The controls fail if multiple people access fund independently. The initial setup entry: Debit Credit Petty Cash (asset) $200 Cash (bank) $200 Nothing hits P&L. The company just moved $200 from a bank account to a physical currency fund. Both are cash-equivalent assets on balance sheet. Recording disbursements from fund Here's where petty cash accounting differs from other transactions. Individual disbursements from petty cash are NOT recorded in general ledger as they happen. Instead, custodian logs each disbursement on a paper or digital petty cash log with: Date Amount Purpose (office supplies, employee reimbursement, courier fee, etc.) Receipt attached (or noted if none is available) Recipient signature (for reimbursements) The general ledger doesn't touch petty cash until replenishment time . This is imprest fund mechanic fund is refilled, and only then does accounting record aggregate expenses. Example: over a month, custodian disburses: $28 for office supplies (Office Depot receipt) $15 for postage stamps (USPS receipt) $42 for employee lunch reimbursement (Chipotle receipt, employee signature) $80 for a courier delivery (invoice with signature) $12 for coffee run for a client meeting (Starbucks receipt) Total disbursed: $177 . Cash remaining in fund: $200 − $177 = $23 . Total receipts and log entries: $177. Cash + receipts should equal $200 (original fund amount). If they don't, something is wrong. Recording replenishment When fund is replenished, aggregate expenses hit general ledger and cash moves back into petty cash fund: Debit Credit Amount Office Supplies Expense $28 Postage Expense $15 Employee Meals Expense $42 Delivery Expense $80 Client Meeting Expense $12 Cash (bank) $177 Note: petty cash is NOT touched in this entry. The petty cash account balance stays at $200 (its original imprest amount). The bank account decreases by $177, and $177 flows to appropriate expense accounts on P&L. Alternative entry if you prefer to route through petty cash (also valid): Debit Credit Petty Cash $177 Cash (bank) $177 Followed by expense recognition. Either method works most bookkeepers use direct expense-recognition method above because it's cleaner. Handling shortages and overages If cash + receipts total doesn't match fund amount, you have a shortage or overage. Cash short (fund is missing money): Debit Cash Short/Over Expense for difference. Common causes: wrong change given, unrecorded disbursement, theft. Cash over (fund has extra money): Credit Cash Short/Over Income (or reduce Cash Short expense). Rare in practice. For a $200 fund with $22 cash and $177 in receipts, total = $199. The fund is short by $1. Replenishment entry: Debit Credit Amount [Various expenses] $177 Cash Short/Over $1 Cash (bank) $178 Persistent shortages (every replenishment cycle is short by $10–$30) point to control problems either poor receipt tracking or petty cash theft. Frequent shortages warrant reviewing custodian assignment and receipt discipline. The petty cash log format A basic log has columns for: Date Description Purpose (Account) Amount Receipt? Recipient 3/2 Office Depot — pens/paper Office Supplies $28 Yes 3/8 USPS stamps Postage $15 Yes 3/15 Chipotle lunch — J. Smith Employee Meals $42 Yes J.S. 3/22 Courier — legal docs Delivery $80 Yes 3/28 Starbucks — client mtg Client Meals $12 Yes Digital petty cash logs in Excel, Google Sheets, or accounting software attachments work fine requirement is that log matches receipts and receipts match aggregate amount taken from cash. Petty cash controls The controls that prevent petty cash from becoming a slush fund: 1. One custodian. Multiple people accessing fund without recording disbursements makes reconciliation impossible. 2. Receipts required for every disbursement. No receipt = no reimbursement. Exceptions for very small amounts (under $5) can be documented on log with a specific explanation. Receipt discipline matters both for internal control and for business expense documentation required at tax time. 3. Signed acknowledgment for employee reimbursements. If Jane got $42 for lunch, Jane signs log entry confirming she received it. 4. Regular replenishment cycles. Monthly is standard for most businesses. Longer intervals cause receipts to pile up and get lost. 5. Reconciliation at each replenishment. Cash + receipts = fund amount. If not, resolve discrepancy before replenishing. 6. Independent verification. Someone other than custodian should periodically count fund. Once a quarter is typical for small businesses. 7. Written petty cash policy. Even a one-page policy stating maximum disbursement amount (e.g., $50/transaction), acceptable purposes, and receipt requirements reduces ambiguity. Month-end reconciliation At month-end, petty cash balance on trial balance should equal fund's imprest amount ($200 in example). If a replenishment happened during month, disbursement expenses hit appropriate expense accounts on that date. The monthly close should confirm: Petty cash trial balance balance = imprest amount Petty cash physical count = trial balance amount No suspense items in Cash Short/Over unless documented If trial balance shows $173 in petty cash when imprest is $200, fund was disbursed but not replenished do replenishment entry before closing period. When to eliminate petty cash Many modern small businesses run without petty cash entirely, using corporate credit cards or expense reimbursement platforms instead. Eliminating petty cash simplifies bookkeeping and reduces theft/loss risk. Signs you should eliminate petty cash fund: Corporate cards or debit cards are widely deployed Reimbursement processes (Expensify, Bill.com, or similar) handle small expenses Petty cash disbursements have dropped to <$50/month Shortages are persistent (control failures) To eliminate: debit Cash (bank) for remaining balance, credit Petty Cash for imprest amount, and offset any residual receipts to expense accounts. Conclusion Petty cash accounting is imprest fund mechanics: fund equals cash + receipts, always. Log every disbursement, reconcile at replenishment, and never touch petty cash account balance until you replenish. Get controls right (one custodian, receipts required, monthly replenishment) and petty cash stays simple. Get them wrong and small amounts add up to real losses over time. FAQ What is petty cash? Physical currency a business keeps on hand for small expenses too minor to justify writing a check or using a corporate card. Typically $100–$500 in fund, managed by a designated custodian under imprest fund system. How do I record petty cash in accounting? Set up a Petty Cash asset account on balance sheet at fund's imprest amount. Individual disbursements are logged on a petty cash log but NOT recorded in general ledger until replenishment. At replenishment, aggregate disbursement amounts hit appropriate expense accounts, and bank balance decreases. What is imprest fund system? An accounting method where petty cash fund is always maintained at a fixed amount. Cash + receipts should always equal imprest amount. Replenishment covers total disbursed (in receipts) since last replenishment. Do I need receipts for petty cash? Yes every disbursement should have a supporting receipt. This is both good internal control and IRS documentation for business expense deductions. Very small disbursements (under $5–$10) can sometimes be documented on log with a specific explanation. How often should I replenish petty cash? Monthly is standard for most small businesses. Larger businesses with heavy petty spending replenish weekly or biweekly. Longer than monthly leads to receipts piling up and getting lost. What is a cash short/over account? An account used to record differences between actual cash on hand and expected cash based on records. Short (missing cash) is an expense; over (extra cash) is income. Persistent shortages indicate control problems. Do I need a petty cash policy? Yes for any business with employees. A basic policy states: maximum disbursement amount, acceptable purposes, receipt requirements, custodian responsibilities, and replenishment cycle. Even a one-page policy reduces ambiguity and enforces discipline. Should I still use petty cash in 2026? Not necessarily. Many small businesses have eliminated petty cash in favor of corporate cards and expense reimbursement platforms. If petty cash disbursements are under $50/month and corporate cards cover most needs, eliminating fund simplifies bookkeeping.

title: Computer Backup vs. Cloud Storage: Which Do You Need?
summary: Learn the difference between computer backup and cloud storage, when to use each, and why many organizations combine both.
body_text: Organizations rarely struggle with a lack of storage options. More often, they struggle with determining which solution best fits the way their data is created, accessed, and protected: backup versus cloud storage. That’s especially true when evaluating backup and cloud storage solutions. The terms are often used interchangeably, but backup and cloud storage are designed to solve different problems. Understanding those differences can help you build a more effective data protection strategy—whether you’re protecting a personal laptop, a growing media archive, employee endpoints, or critical business data. At Backblaze, Computer Backup and B2 Cloud Storage serve distinct purposes. For some customers, one solution is the clear choice. For others, the strongest approach combines both. Before comparing features, it’s helpful to start with a few foundational questions. Three questions to ask before choosing a solution When evaluating Computer Backup and B2 Cloud Storage , consider: Where does your data live today? Who—or what—needs access to it? What event are you trying to recover from? The answers often reveal whether you’re primarily trying to protect a computer, store data in the cloud, or address both needs at the same time. When the goal is protecting a computer For many individuals and businesses, the most important data still lives on laptops, desktops, and attached external drives. A photographer may keep active projects on a workstation. A consultant may store client files locally. A small business may rely on employee laptops as the primary location where work is created and managed. In these situations, the primary concern isn’t cloud infrastructure. It’s protecting the device where the work happens. That’s where Backblaze Computer Backup fits. Computer Backup is designed to automatically protect data stored on a Mac or Windows computer, including connected external hard drives (but not NAS devices). Once installed, it runs continuously in the background, backing up files without requiring users to manually manage folders, storage allocations, or backup schedules. For organizations looking to protect NAS data, B2 Cloud Storage can serve as a backup destination through a variety of supported third-party backup and sync tools. The value becomes clear when something goes wrong: A laptop is stolen. A hard drive fails. Files are accidentally deleted. A ransomware attack impacts local data. A computer needs to be restored after a hardware issue. In each case, the goal is recovery. Computer Backup is often a good fit when: Your most important data lives on a computer. You want automatic, continuous protection. You need to recover from device loss, hardware failure, or accidental deletion. You want a solution that requires minimal administration. Your primary concern is protecting endpoints. For many professionals, families, and small businesses, those requirements align closely with their day-to-day reality. When the goal is storing and managing data in the cloud As organizations grow, data often becomes less tied to individual devices. Files are shared across teams. Backup software protects servers and NAS devices. Applications generate and consume data continuously. Data needs to remain accessible and manageable independent of the original device, whether that’s for long-term retention, team access, application workflows, or infrastructure backups. At that point, the challenge shifts from protecting a computer to managing data itself. That’s where Backblaze B2 Cloud Storage comes in. Unlike endpoint backup, cloud object storage is designed to store data independently of any single device. Data can be uploaded, accessed, managed, shared, and integrated into workflows across users, systems, and applications. Organizations use B2 Cloud Storage for a wide range of use cases, including: Media archives NAS and server backups Ransomware protection Application storage AI and analytics datasets Business continuity and disaster recovery workflows In these environments, accessibility, scalability, and integration often matter just as much as protection. B2 Cloud Storage is often a good fit when: Data needs to exist independently of a specific computer. Multiple users or systems require access. You need API-based access and automation. You use third-party backup software that requires cloud object storage. You need centralized storage for growing datasets. You are building applications or data-driven workflows. The focus isn’t on protecting a device. It’s on providing a durable, accessible home for data. Understanding the data lifecycle One reason organizations often use both backup and cloud storage is that data requirements change over time. Consider a video production team. While a project is actively being edited, the files may live on a workstation and several external drives. During that phase, protecting the editing environment is critical. Once the project is complete, however, the priorities often change. The team may need to retain the content for future revisions, client requests, or compliance purposes. The files are no longer active, but they still need to remain available. The same pattern appears across industries. Architectural firms retain project files after construction is complete. Marketing teams archive campaign assets. Businesses preserve records for operational or regulatory reasons. Not all data serves the same purpose throughout its lifecycle. Active data often benefits from continuous endpoint protection, particularly when it lives on laptops, workstations, or attached drives. As that data ages, becomes shared across teams, or moves into long-term retention, cloud storage often becomes a more appropriate solution. This is one reason many organizations use both Computer Backup and B2 Cloud Storage. The two solutions address different stages of the data lifecycle rather than competing for the same role. When your storage requirements change A common misconception is that organizations eventually “graduate” from backup to cloud storage. In reality, most environments become more complex over time, adding new requirements rather than replacing existing ones. As data volumes grow, teams collaborate across more systems, and retention needs increase, organizations often find themselves adding cloud storage to support those evolving demands. The shift isn’t typically about moving away from backup—it’s about addressing new use cases that emerge as data becomes more distributed, accessible, and valuable to the business. Common signs that additional cloud storage may make sense include: Your data is no longer centered around one device When multiple people need access to the same information, storing everything on a single workstation becomes limiting. You’re building long-term archives Completed projects, historical records, and large media libraries often benefit from dedicated cloud storage. You’re adding automation and integrations Applications, backup platforms, and workflows frequently require API-accessible storage. You’re managing more than endpoints As NAS devices, servers, and infrastructure become part of the environment, storage requirements often extend beyond individual computers. In these scenarios, cloud storage isn’t replacing endpoint backup. It’s addressing new requirements. The blind spot many cloud storage users discover The reverse scenario is also common. An organization adopts cloud storage and establishes a centralized repository for important data, only to discover that important risks still exist at the endpoint level. An employee may accidentally delete a local project folder, lose a laptop, or experience a workstation failure before files have been synchronized elsewhere. Cloud storage protects the data stored in cloud storage, but it does not automatically protect every device where work is created. This is one reason endpoint backup remains an important part of many modern data protection strategies. The risks are different, and each solution is designed to address a different recovery scenario. Why many organizations use both computer backup and cloud storage One of the most persistent myths in data protection is that a single tool should solve every challenge. In practice, resilient environments are typically built in layers, with different solutions addressing different risks and recovery scenarios. Employee laptops may be protected with Computer Backup, while a NAS backs up to B2 Cloud Storage. Completed projects may be archived in the cloud while active work remains protected on local devices. Together, these layers create a more comprehensive approach to protecting data throughout its lifecycle. Example: Creative teams For creative teams, active projects often live on editing workstations and attached storage where they are constantly being updated. Computer Backup helps protect that work in progress, while completed projects can be moved to B2 Cloud Storage for long-term retention, future revisions, or client requests. This approach allows teams to safeguard current work without keeping every finished project on production systems. Example: Growing businesses As businesses grow, their data often becomes distributed across employee devices, shared storage, and business applications. Computer Backup can help protect employee endpoints where work is created, while B2 Cloud Storage provides a centralized location for shared assets, backups, and archives. Together, they support both day-to-day operations and longer-term data retention needs. Example: IT and infrastructure teams IT teams frequently manage a mix of endpoints, servers, NAS devices, and other business systems. In these environments, B2 Cloud Storage often serves as a destination for infrastructure backups, while Computer Backup protects employee devices that may not be covered by server or storage backup workflows. Rather than competing with one another, the two solutions often work together as part of a broader data protection strategy. A quick comparison Question Computer Backup B2 Cloud Storage Is the primary goal protecting a computer? Yes No Is it designed to protect endpoint data automatically? Yes No Is the data primarily tied to a specific device? Yes Not necessarily Is it designed for shared access across users, systems, or applications? No Yes Is API access a core feature? No Yes Can it serve as a destination for third-party backup tools? No Yes Is the primary goal storing and managing cloud-resident data? No Yes Choosing the right solution The decision ultimately comes down to what you’re trying to protect and how your data is used. If your primary concern is recovering files from a lost, stolen, damaged, or compromised computer, Computer Backup is likely the right starting point. If you need scalable cloud storage for archives, applications, infrastructure backups, or shared datasets, B2 Cloud Storage is likely the better fit. And if your environment includes both endpoints and cloud-resident data—as many organizations do—you may benefit from using both. The most effective data protection strategies rarely rely on a single layer. They account for where data is created, where it lives, and how it needs to be recovered. Understanding those requirements is often the first step toward choosing the right solution.

title: Rimini Street Expands C-Suite Leadership for Growth with Appointment of Two Proven Industry Veterans as Chief Operating Officer and Chief Delivery Officer
summary: Keith Costello joins Rimini Street as EVP & Chief Operating Officer (COO); Alexander Guasch joins as EVP & Chief Delivery Officer (CDO).
body_text: Rimini Street appoints Keith Costello as EVP and Chief Operating Officer and Alexander Guasch as EVP and Chief Delivery Officer LAS VEGAS – August 12, 2026 – Rimini Street, Inc. (Nasdaq: RMNI), the Software Support and Agentic AI ERP Company™ and the leading third-party support provider for Oracle, SAP and VMware software, today announced the appointment of Keith Costello as chief operating officer (COO) and Alexander Guasch as chief delivery officer (CDO). New COO Brings Proven Experience Scaling Organizations for Growth Keith Costello brings decades of experience building and scaling global enterprise software and services organizations, including leading teams of tens of thousands and managing businesses generating billions of dollars in revenue. He previously served as president, enterprise applications, technology, consulting and engineering services at DXC Technology and general manager for IBM’s global SAP business unit. Earlier, he completed eight years at SAP in various senior leadership roles, including executive vice president and general manager of business analytics and technology solutions, senior vice president of global field services and chief customer officer. As COO, Costello will own product strategy, determining what products, services and solutions Rimini Street will bring to market. He will also own the professional services sales function and other global business operations, which he will take over from Rimini Street president and CEO Seth Ravin. “It’s an exciting time at Rimini Street. The company has successfully sold billions of dollars of services and built a differentiated offering that helps clients unlock more value from their mission-critical enterprise systems while gaining greater control over their technology roadmaps,” said Costello. “I’m looking forward to working with the global team to scale operations, strengthen execution and support the company’s continued growth worldwide.” New CDO Brings Global Delivery Leadership and Client-Focused Execution Alex Guasch is a seasoned leader with more than 30 years of experience leading integrated global IT service delivery organizations with thousands of professionals. He has led numerous initiatives across enterprise software support, managed services, consulting, modernization, cloud transformation and AI-enabled innovation. Guasch formerly served in senior executive roles at HPE, IBM, VMware and Cognizant and has held leadership positions at Effectual and Optiv. As Rimini Street CDO, he is responsible for the end-to-end development and delivery of all company products, services and solutions worldwide, assuring reliable operational excellence, unparalleled service quality and successful client outcomes. “Client success starts with consistent, high-quality delivery, especially for the mission-critical systems that keep global organizations and government clients running smoothly,” said Guasch. “I’m pleased to join Rimini Street and lead an organization that has a storied reputation as one of the best enterprise software and technology engineering teams in the world, delivering 24/7/365 service globally with an average two-minute response time and client satisfaction ratings of 4.9 out of 5.0.” Rimini Street is firmly focused on executing its operating plan to accelerate revenue growth and increase profitability. These expanded leadership roles strengthen execution, scale global operations and support continued client success. “Keith and Alex bring the global operating experience, execution discipline and client-first leadership to scale our organization with speed and quality,” said Seth Ravin, president and CEO, Rimini Street. “Keith and Alex understand what it takes to run and grow complex technology organizations and deliver extraordinary client outcomes. They are welcome additions to our leadership team as we continue helping clients use technology to lower their total operating costs, improve profitability and enhance competitive advantage.”
